What happened with Alvarez on Sunday?

Alvarez played his first Atletico Madrid match on Sunday after revealing his desire to leave the club during the World Cup.

The Argentine striker wants to leave Diego Simeone's side to join Barcelona. However, Arsenal are also interested in bringing the former Man City striker back to the Premier League.

Barcelona want Alvarez but earlier this summer, Atletico accused the Catalan club of building a "relentless smear campaign" regarding the forward.

"Over the past few months, we've been subjected to a relentless smear campaign against one of our players," wrote Atleti on X.

"Calculated leaks, fake news, constant disrespect, the culé version of the propaganda machine inventing little stories, phone calls before head-to-head clashes.

"But of course, it would never occur to us either to have the vice president of referees on the payroll or to rely on political favours to register players. Respect and values."

With Alvarez wanting to join one of Atleti's closest rivals, the forward was greeted by whistles, boos and jeers from the Atletico Madrid fans on his return to action for the club.

His named was booed as the Atleti team was read out - and Alvarez was sat on the substitutes bench when the first jeers of the afternoon were made. They continued when Alvarez entered the pitch on the 66th minute.

After the game, the Argentina international left the field on his own after the 2-2 home league draw against Villarreal, while his team-mates stayed behind to applaud the fans.

Image: Alvarez was booed by his own supporters on Sunday - and walked off the pitch while his team-mates applauded the crowd

Asked about the situation, Simeone said in his post-match press conference: "People at the club told me that the club decided he shouldn't be near the stands and the fans.

"The decision was made by the club to keep him away and separate him from the rest of the team, so he would come to the locker room instead."

Does this raise Arsenal's chances of signing him?

Just because Alvarez was booed by his own Atletico supporters on Sunday, does not mean Arsenal fans should get excited yet.

Signing the Argentina striker - in what would arguably be the coup of the window - still looks very unlikely to happen before the deadline.

That is because of several obstacles still in their way; primarily the player's heart being set on a move to Barcelona and Atletico Madrid still refusing to sell him with just over a week to go.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking in April, Diego Simeone admitted that Arsenal are interested in Julian Alvarez.

Regardless of the feelings of Atletico fans, the club are digging their heels in, insisting they do not want to sell him to any club; certainly not to Barca and not the Premier League champions nor PSG either.

Arsenal will not completely give up - the door will always be open to a deal from their end right up until September 1 - but until they get an indication that Alvarez has shifted his thinking away from the Nou Camp, there is not much more Andrea Berta and Mikel Arteta can do.

Sky Sports News reported in July that Alvarez's family want to stay in Spain and that remains the case. They are happy and settled and the player's dream has long been to follow in the footsteps of compatriot Lionel Messi and star for Barca.

There is just over a week of the window remaining and anything can happen, but Barcelona will not give up either and it cannot be ruled out that they will not make another push to test Atletico's resolve - which has, until now, held firm.

Do Arsenal need Alvarez?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Friday Night Football panel discuss whether Arsenal are still shy of a world-class attacker that would see them get over the line to win their first UEFA Champions League title.

Arsenal are happy with their squad and showed in their resounding 3-0 opening day win over Coventry that they are in healthy place.

They clearly are now in a position in which signing only the very best will improve on what they have got. Alvarez is that and there are not many others on the market that come close.

However, Gary Neville feels Arsenal getting Alvarez would make them Champions League winners this season. Jamie Carragher feels the Gunners are one stardust signing away from becoming Kings of Europe.

"What a squad [Mikel Arteta] has built," said Neville. "If he puts another forward into that, if they could get Julian Alvarez somehow, that would light this place up as you'd have a world-class striker to go with all the world-class defenders and midfielders.

"They wouldn't just become Premier League title winners they'd go the next step and win a Champions League. It's a massive [few] days [in the transfer window]. He needs a bit of magic up front - someone that can win a game for you when you don't play well."

For the Premier League, Arsenal have shown they are already ahead of their rivals with an opening night victory, with summer signing Christos Tzolis and Martin Odegaard - who missed 30 matches last season - adding another dimension to Arsenal's attack.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Arsenal and Coventry.

Meanwhile, Liverpool, Manchester United and Tottenham all dropped points over the course of the first weekend, while Enzo Maresca admitted his Man City team - who were unconvincing in their late comeback win over Bournemouth - are still a "work in progress."

Arsenal could also move for a left-sided forward - which Alvarez is not - before the transfer deadline, if Gabriel Martinelli moves on this summer.

The Brazilian has been left out of Arsenal's last two matchday squads and has one year left on his deal - plus there is interest from Galatasaray and Saudi Arabia.

Arsenal could also let Gabriel Jesus leave this summer - but will not do so unless a replacement, such as Alvarez, is lined up.

So if Alvarez is unattainable - do Arsenal move elsewhere, or perhaps even not move for a forward at all? Despite being ahead of their rivals, the Premier League champions still face a big final week in the transfer window.

Sports.title: Amorim’s Milan live up to billing as teenage star Cissè upstages signings | Nicky Bandini
Sports.content:
“I love Cissè. I love Cissè.” Ruben Amorim had not yet taken charge of his first competitive game as Milan head coach but already he was furnishing journalists with soundbites and supporters with memes, clippable moments that you just knew we were destined to revisit.

Alphadjo Cissè is a 19-year-old attacking midfielder who signed for Milan from Verona in February but only joined up with them this summer, after completing the season-long loan he had already begun at Catanzaro in Serie B. He scored six goals in 22 games there, missing the second half of the campaign with a thigh injury. Previously he had played a combined 14 minutes for Verona across three substitute appearances in the top flight.

Yet Amorim spoke of Cissè like a man who knew something that the rest of the world doesn’t. More than his words, it was the body language: hands rubbing together in anticipation, lip curled at one corner into an emoji-like version of a smirk.

Cissè would start away to Torino the following evening. Within 75 seconds of kick-off, he had taken the first shot of the game: racing forward to hook a Ruben Loftus-Cheek cross into the side netting from an acute angle beyond the far post.

For an Italian teenager to make Milan’s first XI on the opening weekend was already a significant detail. The scarce opportunities afforded to young domestic talent in Serie A has been a national talking point ever since the Azzurri failed to qualify for a third consecutive men’s World Cup.

Data compiled by Football Benchmark found that Italians who qualified for the under-21 category accounted for only 3.9% of minutes played last season, while foreign players in that age group took 8.2%: “In other words, young foreign players receive more than twice as many opportunities as their Italian counterparts.”

There were signs of a possible shift this weekend. The season began with 21-year-old Pio Esposito delivering a man-of-the-match performance for the champions, Inter, in their 4-1 win over Monza, but he was the exception who stood apart already last year.

More surprising were the new faces popping up elsewhere. Cissè, born in Treviso to Guinean parents, was one of three Italian teenagers on the pitch at the Olympic stadium in Turin, with Diego Mascardi and Alessio Cacciamani, both 19, lining up at goalkeeper and left wing-back for the Granata.

View image in fullscreen Ruben Amorim won his first Serie A match in charge against Ignazio Abate’s Torino. Photograph: Daniele Mascolo/Reuters

The 18-year-olds Matteo Palma (an Italian-German dual national) and Simone Lontani started for Udinese and Parma respectively, and the 19-year-old Mathis Mout for Monza. Even Como, whose project has been criticised for relying almost exclusively on foreign talent, gave Mattia Liberali, 19, some minutes off the bench. It is far too soon to draw conclusions, but certainly a trend worth tracking.

In any case, putting your faith in untested young talent can feel like a greater gamble for a club with Milan’s expectations. After a disappointing fifth-place finish last season under Massimiliano Allegri, the Rossoneri have spent big – appointing Amorim and then dropping a club-record €74m to sign Gonçalo Ramos from Paris Saint-Germain, as well as another €50m on the midfielder Diego Moreira from Strasbourg and €30m on the defender Mario Gila from Lazio.

Amorim has not shied away from ambition, saying his goal is to win the Scudetto, even while acknowledging it may take time to bridge the gap to Inter. More than that, he has won over fans with the promise of a front-footed team who will seek to set the tempo and dictate how games are played – a welcome change from the caution and reactivity of Allegri.

There were promising performances in pre-season – not least the 4-2 win over Amorim’s last club, Manchester United, with Cissè on the scoresheet. But friendlies are not the real thing. Sunday’s visit to a Torino side undergoing a renewal of their own under a new head coach, and former Milan player, Ignazio Abate, was always going to be a fascinating first challenge.

Ramos and Gila started, at centre-forward and on the right of defence. Moreira, who only completed his move on 19 August, stayed on the bench. Cissè was the other truly new face, playing to the left of Ramos in a 3-4-2-1, though Yunus Musah and the right wing-back Samuel Chukwueze were also returning after spending last season out on loan.

Amorim’s approach lived up to billing. From the start, Milan dominated the ball and the pitch – claiming more than 70% of first-half possession while outshooting their opponents by 11 to one. And yet, they struggled to break Torino down in the final third. Aside from one solo effort by Chukwueze, who dribbled in from the right and forced a save from Mascardi, they had rarely looked like scoring.

Quick Guide Serie A results Show Parma 0-1 Cagliari, Genoa 0-2 Napoli, Udinese 1-1 Como, Inter 4-1 Monza, Torino 1-2 Milan, Atalanta 2-1 Sassuolo, Venezia 0-2 Lecce, Frosinone 0-1 Juventus Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Cissè thought he had earned Milan a penalty after the interval, when his cross struck the arm of Nikola Vlasic. That the VAR booth did not call the referee, Luca Zufferli, to take a second look may be an early indicator – together with incidents from other games – of a shift in approach under the new refereeing designator, Daniele Orsato. He has stated a desire to “put referees back at the centre of the match” and return to the idea that technology should only be used for those elusive “clear and obvious” mistakes.

Torino were growing into the game. But that might also have been their undoing. In the 64th minute, Musah turned his man in midfield, surging into space left open by the home team’s press. He fed Adrien Rabiot, a second-half substitute, on the right. The Frenchman crossed to Cissè, who brought the ball down with his waist and curled a half volley into the far corner. The teenager slid to his knees as he celebrated in front of the away fans.

Within moments it was 2-0, Rabiot himself converting a Chukwueze delivery. Torino kept battling, and Scotland’s Ché Adams scored the best goal of the game in injury time, an outrageously nonchalant right-foot volley over his own left shoulder. But the three points went to Milan.

Cissè laughed when the interviewer from Dazn asked him at full time what he thought about Amorim’s professions of love. “It makes me happy,” he said. “But I didn’t hear the press conference. All my friends told me about it instead.”

View image in fullscreen Alphadjo Cissè’s half volley gives Milan the lead in Turin. Photograph: Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images

He was still recovering from injury when he first joined up with Milan this summer. Cissè said he had tried to watch training as closely as possible, getting to know what the head coach wanted. Still, he acknowledged, it was “beyond a dream” to get to start, and score, in the season opener.

The numbers say he is the youngest Italian to score for Milan since Patrick Cutrone in 2017, as well as the first Italian to score for them on a debut Serie A start since Daniel Maldini in 2021. Those names should remind everyone not to get ahead of themselves. Cutrone, now 28, was a substitute for Monza this weekend and has only reached double figures for goals once in a top-flight season. Maldini, 24, has played for seven clubs since 2022, and begins this campaign with Cagliari.

But Amorim clearly thinks highly of Cissè, who has represented Italy at various age categories up to under-21, saying he looked at times in the first-half like the most experienced player on the pitch.

The head coach, conducting his interviews mostly in English, said Milan have “a lot to improve”, acknowledging both their struggles to break Torino down early on and the way they faded at the end. “[But] the first thing is also win. That is the most important thing. We talk about ways of playing, but there is one goal in calcio. Vincere.”

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from opening weekend of the season
Sports.content:
1 Wright laments Martinelli treatment

Arsenal’s treatment of Gabriel Martinelli has been questioned by Ian Wright after the Brazil forward was left out of their squad for Friday’s opening game against Coventry. Martinelli turned down a move to Galatasaray last week after Arsenal had agreed a fee with the Turkish club and the former striker Wright revealed on Sky Sports after the Coventry game that no one at the club has spoken to the 25-year-old to discuss his future. “I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say: ‘Yeah, it’s time for him to move him on.’ But there’s ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave,” said Wright. “He’s done enough with this squad to be treated with a little bit more respect than he’s being treated with at the moment.” Ed Aarons

Quick Guide Play our football trivia game, On the ball Show The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues? Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

2 Has Watkins tarnished legacy?

It was only one game after 278 for Aston Villa, accumulated over the previous six seasons – a period in which Ollie Watkins has scored 108 goals and made himself one of the most popular players in the club’s Premier League history. But the rules are the rules. Nobody can refuse to play and emerge without a mark against their character. This is the charge against Watkins, brought in none-too-subtle fashion by Unai Emery after Villa’s 4-0 defeat at Brighton – a match that Watkins missed as he considers an approach from Al-Hilal. We do not yet have Watkins’s side of the story. Or that of his agent. But given Emery had no other available No 9, it feels pretty clear the manager did not choose to omit Watkins. Villa claim they are not close to any agreement with Al-Hilal, having rejected more than one offer from them. Perish the thought that this could drag on. Villa have one more game before the window shuts – against Arsenal at home next Monday night. David Hytner

View image in fullscreen Unai Emery did nothing to deny that Ollie Watkins had refused to play for Villa in their sobering defeat. Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty Images

3 United falter as No 9 options look thin

Michael Carrick was limited in his options during Manchester United’s opener because Benjamin Sesko was unable to feature at any point in pre-season but Matheus Cunha was completely ineffective as a false 9. Hull’s back three enjoyed a very quiet lunchtime as they returned to the Premier League. Cunha did not embrace the physical battle and went missing, leaving United with barely any presence in the final third as they failed to threaten their opponents. Sesko was brought on to change the dynamic but was equally ineffectual, while his fellow striker Joshua Zirkzee was left on the bench, implying how little trust the coaches have in him. Carrick needs to get Sesko up to speed and sell Zirkzee soon, freeing up funds to find a better alternative if United are to compete this season, especially with the false 9 tactic looking flawed. Will Unwin

4 Tigers delight in Tzolakis’s debut

Manchester United were impressively unthreatening in their approach to losing at Hull. There was the odd half-baked attempt at scoring or putting a cross into a dangerous area but nothing that made the highlights reel. This was unfortunate for the Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, who had an impressive, if somewhat uncomplicated, debut between the sticks. United should have made a greater effort to test the £20m signing from Olympiakos. What duties the Greek international was forced to do were carried out with ease, instilling confidence in the defence in front of him. If he continues to look so calm and assured, Tzolakis could prove himself one of the smartest signings of the season. “We bought him and we spent some money there,” Sergej Jakirovic said. “He’s a national-team player of Greece, an Olympiakos player. If you’re following Greek football, Olympiakos, it’s a huge stress, huge pressure there, and he’s used to it. For him, I think this is like a cup of tea.” WU

5 Cherki’s crucial cameo after disquiet

Rayan Cherki wrested the three points in a cameo that consisted of the corner for Marc Guéhi’s equaliser and the cute pass for Josko Gvardiol’s winner. Enzo Maresca gave an insight into the Frenchman’s disquiet at not starting. “Rayan is quite a nice and clear boy, if he is not happy he wants to show it. If he’s next to me and he’s not happy, you all realise that he is not happy because he is doing anything just to show that he is not happy. I know that he was not happy today but at the end I had to take a decision,” said the manager. Jamie Jackson

6 Sangaré shines against big spenders

At a time when some Premier League are willing to spend more than £100m on midfielders there is unlikely to be a better bargain than Mamadou Sangaré. Brentford’s new signing was excellent for Lens last season and was outstanding on his debut against Tottenham. Sangaré dominated midfield, even with Spurs able to field upwards of £175m worth of talent in Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes, and his performance raised the question of why the league’s bigger clubs are not willing to look further afield for signings. Brentford, after all, paid only £39m for Sangaré. Yet it seems inevitable there will be clubs willing to pay double the price if he has a good first season in England. Jacob Steinberg

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

7 Isak struggles on return to Newcastle

As gut-wrenching as it must have been for Newcastle fans to see their side concede a stoppage-time penalty to Liverpool, at least they can take comfort that it wasn’t Alexander Isak that scored the Reds’ dramatic equaliser from 12 yards. The former Newcastle striker had a torrid time on his return to St James’ Park – booed at every touch, crunched by Lewis Hall in the tackle and sending his only real chance of note into orbit – but he would surely have fancied taking his revenge with the last kick of the game before Dominik Szoboszlai converted the 99th-minute spot-kick. Worryingly, Isak is lacking the fluency that convinced Liverpool to spend £125m last summer and with Hugo Ekitiké still sidelined with a long-term injury, Andoni Iraola doesn’t have a natural replacement at No 9. If Liverpool are to be successful this season, Isak has to turn it on. Michael Butler

View image in fullscreen Alexander Isak watches the ball during his return to Tyneside. Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty Images

8 Ipswich combat set pieces with O’Shea

A defensive tactical shift from the Ipswich Town manager, Gary O’Neil, demonstrated the changing nature of the Premier League. O’Neil, an astute reader of the game, chose to play the tall centre-back Dara O’Shea at right-back to counter the threat of set pieces that have become so prevalent, in Ipswich’s surprise win against Sunderland. “Aerially the Premier League is such a test now, from long throws and set pieces,” O’Neil said. “To have three centre-half types in your back four helps us from set pieces, size-wise.” In the first season since Pep Guardiola departed, the top flight is already shifting away from his neat, passing football to a different beast. Sam Cunningham

9 Dewsbury-Hall on path to complete midfielder

David Moyes felt his young Everton team might have been uncomfortable chasing the game against Crystal Palace and were therefore indebted to Jordan Pickford’s save from Eddie Nketiah, plus Jean-Philippe Mateta’s finishing, for not having to do so. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall’s guidance was instrumental too. The performance of both teams altered once the midfielder imposed himself, while his superb strike beyond Dean Henderson underlined the quality of a player who will be crucial to Everton’s aspirations. “I want to be better than last season,” said Dewsbury-Hall, who delivered eight goals and four assists in his first Premier League campaign at Everton. “That’s not just goals and assists, it’s my overall play. A couple of years ago I probably wasn’t getting goals and assists but was influential in play. I want to mix that together and when you do that that’s when you become a complete midfielder. I know I have the ability to do it so fingers crossed I do.” Andy Hunter

10 Farke hopes Leeds can cement status

Optimism abounds at Leeds. An encouraging opening-day victory at Nottingham Forest gave credence to the idea that Daniel Farke’s side are capable of cementing their place in the league. Last season, survival was the aim but after investing about £80m to sign James Trafford, Tarik Muharemovic and Nico Elvedi, plus Harry Wilson on a free, they are seeking to build on a 14th-placed finish. Leeds and Forest, who meet again in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday, have both been linked with a move for Chelsea’s Liam Delap; a striker to share the load with Dominic Calvert-Lewin would surely elevate Farke’s side. “If we want to establish ourselves and after a few years perhaps speak about something else, then we need to add individual quality,” Farke said. “The last time this club was able to have two solid seasons at this level, you will perhaps find it in black-and-white photos.” Ben Fisher

Sports.title: EFL and Scottish league pushing to stop illegal broadcast of matches in Russia
Sports.content:
The English Football League and Scottish Professional Football League have launched investigations and are considering legal action after discovering that television coverage of their matches has been broadcast in Russia this season.

Football TV, a Russian subscription and streaming service, has broadcast numerous games from the opening two rounds of the EFL, as well as Scottish Premiership matches featuring Celtic, Rangers and Hearts.

The EFL and SPFL stopped broadcasting in Russia in March 2022 after the previous month’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and have not sold rights packages in the country since, so the live footage of games appears to have been obtained and televised illegally.

Quick Guide How do I 

Until Russia’s full-scale invasion the EFL had a rights contract with Football TV, and the Scottish Premiership was broadcast on Match TV.

The Premier League suspended its broadcasts in Russia at the same time, with its rights held by Okko Sport.

The EFL contacted Football TV last week after being alerted that several games, including Cardiff’s 1-1 draw with Wrexham last Monday and Watford’s 2-1 win over Southampton the previous day, were shown in Russia, but despite this complaint the broadcaster also aired live coverage of West Ham v Charlton and West Brom v Burnley this past weekend.

Those matches were listed as test events, raising concerns that Football TV may also plan to show illegal content from the Premier League.

Several Scottish Premiership matches were shown over the past two weekends, with the broadcasts promoted on Football TV’s Telegram channel.

The EFL and the SPFL’s priority is to ensure the broadcasts stop, which is being pursued, and they are seeking to discover the source of the pirated content.

Both organisations are understood to reserve the right to take legal action against Football TV and whoever is supplying it with access to their matches.

An SPFL source said the league was investigating the matter in conjunction with its broadcasting distribution rights holder, Infront.

The EFL and SPFL declined to comment.

Sports.title: Ceferin brands Infantino’s failed World Cup plan as ‘even worse than the Super League’
Sports.content:
The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has described Gianni Infantino’s doomed attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup as “even worse than the Super League plan” and warned his embattled Fifa counterpart that he will face an opponent if he runs for re-election next March.

Ceferin has led Uefa’s firm collective stance against the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, which was shelved amid widespread opposition at the start of August. Uefa are pushing for Infantino to quit, also drawing on support from Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, and are yet to drop a threat to boycott Fifa competitions while talks are under way with Concacaf to set up a combined Nations League tournament.

In an interview with the podcast The Rest is Politics: Leading, Ceferin denounced Infantino’s project as more damaging than the breakaway Super League that was shelved in 2021 after large-scale protests. “I think this plan is even worse than the Super League plan,” he said. “In the first case, super-important clubs wanted to do their own league, which is wrong and would destroy football. But in this case, football would be literally sold.

“I’m absolutely sure that the [FFE] plan is dead. For me, the most important thing is that we stopped another try to sell the sport. It’s hard to imagine what kind of people would sell the sport that belongs to everyone.”

Earlier this month it was reported that Infantino had held talks about running the Super League under Fifa branding. Ceferin is confident that any revival of that plan would be decades away. “It might happen in 20 years, you never know, but for now we cooperate with everyone in a great way. I’m sure it cannot happen in the next 10 years,” he said.

Infantino spent much of the weekend courting support from Concacaf members at a meeting in the Dominican Republic, infuriating many of those present. Ceferin, who revealed the pair had not been in contact since the FFE scandal broke, believes the Fifa president’s path to survival is narrowing.

“I didn’t speak with him, he didn’t contact me since this happened,” he said. “But there are two options. One option is that he realises that he doesn’t have the support, and that’s not only political support of the ones who vote, but the political support of the football community, the political support of fans, the political support of the players, former players, coaches.

“And the second option [is] that he goes to the elections in March, but in that case, I think he will have a candidate against him. I don’t know yet who.” The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, has been tipped as a potential opponent for Infantino if he chooses to run in Rabat.

Ceferin has proponents of his own but ruled out making his own bid for the Fifa presidency. “My credibility is much, much, much higher if I’m not interested in the position,” he said. The Slovenian is expected to run unopposed for a fourth term at the helm of Uefa, with the election due next April.

Asked whether Infantino had become too close to Donald Trump, with whom he forged a close relationship before the recent World Cup, Ceferin said: “To be honest, I think you are naive if you think that a politician like that, or any politician, is your good friend. The moment you are a problem, you stop being a friend of a politician.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That friendship came under the spotlight last month when Trump said he had called Infantino to ask for a review of the red card given to the US striker Folarin Balogun, whose ban for the last-16 tie against Belgium was later suspended. “That was more than shocking,” Ceferin said. “We have rules and if you don’t respect your own rules, then the game doesn’t make any sense. That’s shocking and, trust me, almost everybody was shocked. Just not everybody dared to speak.”

Meanwhile, in a fresh show of European opposition to Infantino, the six Nordic football associations issued a statement saying they had “lost confidence in the Fifa president and have serious concerns about the governance and high-level decision making of the organisation”. They asked for binding assurances that Fifa will never again “open its governance or competitions to private ownership” and called for a full third-party review into the FFE scheme.

Earlier in August the Norwegian Football Federation was the first member association to call directly for Infantino to step down.

Infantino travelled straight from the Dominican Republic to Paris on Sunday, attending the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup. Television footage showed him exchanging greetings with the president of France, Emmanuel Macron.

Sports.title: Chelsea change course with Alonso primed to banish the chaos of youth
Sports.content:
It is a necessary reset. Although it would be pushing it to say that Chelsea have switched from development centre to retirement home, even after the signings of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck, there has been a clear shift in strategy this summer. Some grownups are in the room at last and, for Xabi Alonso, the hope is that bringing in more experience will help a squad still packed with youngsters show more composure when adversity strikes.

Discipline was a problem for Chelsea last season: they had 11 red cards in all competitions and a lot of the wounds were self-inflicted. Chelsea were impetuous, on the receiving end of too many bookings for dissent and prone to collapsing at the first sign of trouble. No wonder Alonso, who was the epitome of calm during his playing career, has focused on maintaining “emotional control” before opening his tenure as manager with Monday’s trip to Fulham.

It will be a test of Chelsea’s mentality. Craven Cottage has been the setting for some spectacular implosions during the BlueCo era, the path to two 2-1 victories for Fulham over their neighbours smoothed by João Félix earning a red card on his Chelsea debut in 2023 and by Marc Cucurella getting himself sent off after 22 minutes last season.

Chelsea need to change, and hiring Alonso was a tacit admission that their approach required fine-tuning. Internally there was a recognition that the club had undervalued the importance of aura when it came to hiring coaches.

They blundered with Graham Potter and Liam Rosenior, neither of whom were capable of standing the heat. Alonso is a different breed. The 44-year-old burnished his reputation by leading Bayer Leverkusen to the Bundesliga title in 2024 and he wowed Chelsea during his discussions over the role, so much so that they broke with the past by naming him manager rather than head coach.

Now the players can look to the dugout and see an authority figure. Alonso has not seized absolute power – he is still part of a wider structure, collaborating with an extensive recruitment team – but there is no doubt that his arrival has lent credibility to a project that was in danger of falling apart when the Rosenior experiment ended.

View image in fullscreen Liam Rosenior struggled at Stamford Bridge, lasting less than four months. Photograph: Javier García/Shutterstock

Of course, it remains to be seen if success in Germany means Alonso can dominate in England. Leverkusen was special but Real Madrid left him with a scar. Then again, the Bernabéu is not exactly where managers go to develop. It makes Álvaro Arbeloa, who stepped in at Madrid after Alonso’s sacking last season, a similar unknown after replacing Marco Silva at Fulham.

Yet there is optimism around Chelsea. Can they mount a title challenge for the first time in a decade? There is a lot of ground to make up after finishing 10th last season. Weaknesses linger, particularly in goal, and a push for the top four looks likelier.

However, no European football could be a blessing, giving Alonso more time in training. He looks tactically flexible. Chelsea switched between a back four and a back three during pre-season. Cucurella has joined Madrid but Marco Palestra, signed from Atalanta for £43m, and Pep Chavarría, a £16.3m arrival from Rayo Vallecano, could play as wingbacks.

The recruitment looks purposeful. After years of buying promising youngsters Chelsea have targeted ready-made players. Maxence Lacroix, the 26-year-old France centre-back, is a sensible signing from Crystal Palace. Morgan Rogers, signed from Aston Villa for £117m, can play in a range of positions in attacking midfield and could form an exciting partnership with a rested Cole Palmer, who has a point to prove after missing out on England’s World Cup squad.

There is talent here. There always has been, though. The flaw has more been around mindset. It is a footballing norm to have wise heads around to protect young players. Chelsea went too far in the opposite direction and it is one of the first areas Alonso has addressed.

Perhaps he has heard the tale of one of his predecessors having to deal with a player prioritising a haircut over a team meeting. Either way it did not feel on brand when Chelsea made an unsuccessful attempt to sign the 33-year-old Granit Xhaka from Sunderland in June. Yet it underlined their desire for more leadership and the box was ticked when Welbeck, 35, joined from Brighton in a cut-price deal and Henderson, 36, was brought in on a free transfer from Brentford.

View image in fullscreen New signing Danny Welbeck offers experience, maturity and a reliable source of goals. Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty Images

They could be canny moves. Perhaps there is an element of overkill, a sense of Chelsea taking their new direction too far, but Welbeck and Henderson still have something to offer. Welbeck scored 13 league goals for Brighton last season and will provide cover for João Pedro up front, while Henderson did not look out of place for Brentford and, according to Jude Bellingham, is someone coaching staff will always go to when there are problems to resolve.

Alonso needs order. There are still rumblings of instability off the pitch, with Todd Boehly and Mark Walter looking to sell their stakes in the club to the majority shareholder, Clearlake Capital. Quiet is rare. Chelsea need to shift a host of players before the transfer window shuts and questions hover over Enzo Fernández, who favours a reunion with Enzo Maresca at Manchester City.

There has been a lot of noise around Fernández. The midfielder has made no secret of his desire to leave but speaking out so much when Chelsea were wounded underlined the decline in standards. Alonso needs leaders. He needs trust. He still has to prove the hype is justified but his attempts to change Chelsea’s mentality is an encouraging first step.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Alvarez set for Arsenal after being booed at Atlético?
Sports.content:
Booing Julián Alvarez during Atlético Madrid’s draw with Villarreal on Sunday has seemingly convinced the Argentina forward to consider joining Arsenal in the window. The former Manchester City man has been kept out of the reaches of Barcelona, who may not have the funds to complete the signing, whereas the Gunners have plenty of cash to splash.

Alejandro Balde was left out of the Barcelona squad as they roared past Elche, as the Catalan club open the door for a move to Manchester United. A new left-back should solve all of the problems at Old Trafford, that’s for sure.

Jarrod Bowen has committed his future to West Ham, despite them being relegated and starting the Championship season in desperate fashion. Despite all that, perhaps he will be tempted by a £50m bid from Crystal Palace after a welcome to the Championship to forget? The Eagles were blunt at Everton over the weekend and could be about to initiate panic stations by splashing out quite severely for the Hammers skipper.

Losing 4-0 at Brighton is not going to do much for morale but it will make a team take drastic action in the market. Aston Villa have lined up Joel Ordóñez to solve all of their problems for the remainder of the season, if Club Brugge are willing to sell the centre-back.

There is only one way to bounce back from losing at Ipswich and that is to chase a £34m Barcelona player. Sunderland have tracked Marc Casadó throughout the summer and could be about to pounce for the 22-year-old, who has also been linked with most of the Premier League in recent weeks.

It is difficult to decipher if Cruzeiro’s Jonathan Jesus would sign for Strasbourg or Chelsea, but the talk in Brazil is that ownership group BlueCo want the 22-year-old centre-back. Real Betis, Valencia and Benfica are equally keen, adding a bit of jeopardy to the chase.

With Chelsea always looking to move on a few players, they will be ecstatic to hear that Napoli are contemplating a move for the striker Marc Guiu. Whether the Italians are up for splurging £25m on the Spaniard remains to be seen because the Serie A club currently believe the Blues’ valuation is a touch on the high side.

As alluded to, it was a fantastic start to the season for Hull on Saturday when they gave Manchester United a bit of a shooing. To help build on that, they have agreed a £15.4m deal to sign forward Mohamed-Ali Cho from Nice.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 3: Birmingham City
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 12th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 1st (WSL2)

Prospects

Founding members of the Women’s Super League when it launched in 2011, Birmingham are back in the top flight after four years in the second tier, having won promotion as WSL2 champions on the final day of last season. After a decent summer transfer window, Birmingham look to have a fighting chance of staying up, and perhaps even surprising a few teams, while off the pitch they are the best-equipped of the three promoted sides to cement themselves in the top division.

Forwards Lily Crosthwaite and Wilma Leidhammar and defender Neve Herron, are all 23-years-old and likely to continue improving. Birmingham have also added players with WSL experience, such as the former Brighton goalkeeper Sophie Baggaley and the centre-back Millie Turner.

Inconsistency was nearly their downfall last season; they won the most games in WSL2, but also lost six times. They delivered under pressure, boosted by the performances of Leidhammar after her club-record arrival in January, ensuring they avoided a repeat of the heartbreak of 12 months earlier when they missed out on promotion on the final day. Nonetheless, Birmingham are still a long way off from the days when they were runners-up in the top tier and their first two away fixtures are against Manchester City and Chelsea. They also host fellow promoted sides Crystal Palace and Charlton relatively early in the campaign and those home fixtures could be key to building confidence.

Off-field picture

Birmingham’s women’s team were sold to the club’s ownership group in February, with Shelby Companies Limited – an affiliate of Knighthead Capital Management – owning 97%. The remaining 3% was purchased by investors including the former England midfielder Karen Carney and the four-time grand slam tennis champion Kim Clijsters. The club appear to be in a relatively healthy position with ambitious owners determined to reestablish the 2012 FA Cup winners as a regular, competitive presence in the WSL. They train at the recently renovated Knighthead Performance Centre, on the same site as the men’s team’s former Wast Hills training base, with a new gym among other extensive refurbishments.

The manager

Amy Merricks has been in charge since April 2024 She holds a Uefa Pro Licence and was 30 years old when she was appointed by Birmingham. She has previously coached within the England youth setup as well as at Gillingham, Millwall and Brighton, where was stepped up to be interim manager three times.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Lisa Naalsund arrives from Manchester United to boost Birmingham’s midfield. Photograph: DeFodi Images/Getty Images

Birmingham have recruited players with international experience, including the Canada defender Marie Levasseur from Montpellier, but their two most eyebrow-raising additions are Turner and Lisa Naalsund from Manchester United. They were starting members of United’s FA Cup-winning side of 2024 and played in a Women’s Champions League quarter-final as recently as April. Naalsund will be an influential force in the midfield – she has won 39 caps and was part of Norway’s squad at last year’s Euros.

Stat attack

Birmingham topped WSL2 last season despite not scoring the most goals or conceding the fewest. One stat they led was big chances, Opta’s metric for opportunities where it is reasonable to expect the attacker to score. While their tally will be much harder to repeat in the top flight, their attacking process looks in good order.

Set for a breakthrough

There is plenty of excitement at Birmingham about another of their new signings, the 19-year-old France youth forward Chancelle Effa Effa, who arrived from Le Havre for a fee understood to be about €120,000 (£100,000) this month. She broke into Le Havre’s first team at the age of 15 and scored 17 times in 28 games for France’s Under-17 and Under-19 teams, having helped France win 2023’s Under-17 Euros.

What they say …

“We know it’s going to be a massive challenge, but it’s a challenge that, as players, you thrive upon. As long as we can take that togetherness, that relentlessness, into the games, I’m sure we’re going to be just fine” – Chelsea Cornet.

Where are they playing their home games?

Birmingham play their home fixtures at St Andrew’s, which has been the women’s team’s home since 2021. They set a club record attendance for a women’s game there on the final day of the 2024-25 season – 8,749. Long-term, the club have announced plans to build a new women’s team stadium as part of the ‘Sports Quarter’, which also includes the proposed 62,000-seater men’s team Powerhouse Stadium as well as an indoor arena, training ground facilities and a new railway station.

Sports.title: ‘Call his agent’: Emery feels Watkins should explain absence from Villa’s rout by Brighton
Sports.content:
Unai Emery did nothing to deny that Ollie Watkins had refused to play for Aston Villa in their sobering 4-0 defeat by Brighton at the Amex on Sunday. The head coach had a selection crisis up front with Brian Madjo and Tammy Abraham injured. However, he did not include Watkins in the matchday squad as the England striker considers a move to Al-Hilal in Saudi Arabia.

Emery was forced to rely on the attacking midfielder Emiliano Buendía as an emergency striker and his team disappeared without trace on the south coast. They were 4-0 down after 31 minutes and had their new signing João Gomes sent off on his debut in the 40th minute. Gomes kicked up and out at the Brighton striker Georginio Rutter after being dispossessed by him.

Al-Hilal have made a number of bids for Watkins, all of which have been rejected. It is understood the 30-year-old is open to the move and Emery talked on Friday like a manager who was realistic about the sale happening. Villa would plainly like to replace Watkins should he depart as they approach the end of another difficult summer window. They have already sold Ezri Konsa, Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne and Youri Tielemans, while they are expected to move on Emiliano Martínez.

Emery was asked why he had not picked Watkins against Brighton. “This question is for him,” he said. “I can answer only with my silence.” Emery was then asked if Watkins had refused to play, to which he said: “I think you can call him and you can call his agent and he can respond.”

The Guardian have contacted Watkins’s agent for comment.

“He [Watkins] can only explain his answer, I can’t,” Emery added, after being asked if he felt let down by Watkins.

Emery reported that Madjo would be out for “two weeks more … more or less” while attacking midfielder Johan Manzambi – who has been the club’s marquee summer signing – would “need maybe some days more [than that]”. He was unclear about a timeframe for Abraham’s return.

Quick Guide How do I 

Emery talked up the resistance of his players in the second half against Brighton and said he was optimistic about finding solutions for the season ahead. But he returned to the difficult preparations for the opening fixture, noting that: “Two strikers are injured and another striker gives his answer.”

The head coach added: “This problem [with the transfer market] … we had every season and every season we overcame it. It’s something we have to accept and always we reacted, especially the players. This is something hard for us every year but we are calm. With this result, it’s more difficult to explain but calm, work, be positive and find solutions for the next week and after the transfer window.”

Sports.title: New £18m Chelsea signing's WAG left terrified and trapped by a SQUIRREL - after ChatGPT told her it could attack - amid struggles with move to London
Sports.content:
New £18m Chelsea signing's WAG left terrified and trapped by a SQUIRREL - after ChatGPT told her it could attack - amid struggles with move to London

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The girlfriend of one of Chelsea's new stars came face-to-face with a sinister squirrel on one of her first days in London.

And the encounter left her shook like never before, to the extent that the ordeal required a 90-second TikTok debrief.

Influencer Pawgli, who has been dating £18million full-back Pep Chavarria since November, has moved to the English capital despite severe reservations over the switch.

In her previous videos, she spoke about the 'scary' prospect of leaving Madrid and the opportunities and family she has there.

Pawgli, 27, has more than 1.1 million followers on TikTok and creates fashion, beauty, and lifestyle content in Spanish.

But after taking the plunge with Chavarria, she has encountered a foe more fearsom ethan she could ever imagine: a furry chipmunkesque rodent, positioned menacingly on the path.

'How a 50-minute walk ended up taking an hour and a half... because of a squirrel,' she began in a TikTok video.

The influencer girlfriend of a new Chelsea star has recounted her horror at meeting a squirrel

She shared a picture of the offending rodent with her 1.1 million TikTok followers

Pawgli, the girlfriend of new Chelsea signing Pep Chavarria, was torn about moving to London

'But I was going to tell you about the other day when I made a vlog for you going to get my nails done in London for the first time. You have no idea everything that happened to me.

'Of course, we're still in the hotel because they don't give Pepo the house until the 28th.

'So I went to get my nails done; Google Maps showed 50 minutes to get to the nail place, but I thought, "go on, I'll walk a bit, get to know the area, etc."

'I had been walking for 45 minutes, okay? Because it took me through places that were just woods, woods, woods, and surrounded by lakes... super pretty landscapes, yes, but all forest, as if I were in the Hansel and Gretel movie.

'All kinds of animals popped up, and when I had only 20 minutes left to reach the nail place - and I was almost out of the forest because I could already see civilization - a squirrel in the middle of the path wasn't moving. Staring at me like this...

'I asked ChatGPT, "Do squirrels attack?" And it said, "Yes." And I... backed away.

'Wait until it leaves and don't pass through there," etc. That's what ChatGPT told me. I waited for about 10 or 15 minutes... and the squirrel wouldn't leave.

'I decided to turn all the way back the way I came, and I saw another path - also all forest -and I said, "Okay, I'll go through here," and the whole route recalculated, making me walk an hour and a half instead of 50 minutes.

The duo have been together since November last year but she may decide to continue the relationship long-distance

She broke down in tears, has described the situation as 'scary', and says she is 'panicking'

Perhaps the influencer has not encountered many squirrels before in Madrid, where their population has dwindled.

It is an uncomfortable start for Pawgli, who had been seriously weighing up whether or not to join her footballer boyfriend in London or continue their relationship long-distance from Madrid.

In one video, she broke down in tears at the situation.

She said: 'By moving to London, I'm kind of giving up on doing 100 per cent of my job. He has his job, I have mine; he earns his money, I earn mine. Nobody lives off anyone else; I don't live off my boyfriend.

'Therefore, by not living in Madrid, I'm losing opportunities - opportunities for me to keep growing in this - because absolutely everything is in Madrid.

'I want to keep holding on to my Spanish audience. I don't know how to speak English, at least right now, though I know I'll have to learn.

'But no matter how much English I know, I don't want to change my audience and have an English-speaking audience. I want to stay with my Spanish audience, which is why, all things considered, living in Madrid is so good for me.

'As someone who is ultra mega family-oriented and super sensitive, moving to a country I don't know, where I have nothing, no life, no job, and where I'm going to lose career opportunities...

Pawgli says she does not want to abandon her Spanish-speaking audience

The 27-year-old is 'mega-happy' for her partner but did not want to leave her family behind

'And I'm doing it out of love, because I love my partner and want to build a future and a family with him.'

Pawgli denied that she had broken down in tears over the prospect of losing work and going to free events in Madrid.

But in another video, she did clearly indicate that she is in some turmoil about the change.

Chavarria, a late bloomer who only made his LaLiga debut aged 24, has spent the last four seasons with Madrid-based club Rayo Vallecano.

Pawgli said: 'I have my life in Madrid; I have my job in Madrid, which luckily is going very, very well. I have projects, I have all the brands I work with there, I have daily events, I have my sister, my family, my friends. I have a life where I feel fortunate - it's a dream life for me and one that cost me a lot to build.

'So, when you start a relationship and your partner gets an opportunity like this, you're obviously ultra-mega happy for him and super proud of him, but you also have to sit down with yourself and think, "Okay, now what do I do?"

'And I swear until recently I was completely convinced that I wasn't going to move in with him. He has his life in London right now, I have mine in Madrid; I respect his life, he respects mine, and whenever possible, we'll see each other.

'A long-distance relationship. Something I would've never considered in my life, but if one thing was clear to me, it's that I will never in my life depend on anyone or live off anyone. I have my own income, and that's how it'll always be.

Pawgli, who has 1.1 million TikTok followers, insists that she wants a family with Chavarria

'All of this is scary for someone who has everything in Madrid. Right now I'm panicking, honestly, because I know it's a very tough decision.

'I also want to be able to experience this with Pep, because if I met my boyfriend and he's been here in Madrid for like 4 years and I met him, and precisely this year he has to go to London, maybe it's because fate also wants me to go.

'Because I'm obviously going to make content for you wherever I go, and being in London I can do even more, right? Because there are things there that aren't in Spain.

'I have a thousand ideas in my head because I can't stop thinking, honestly.'

Pawgli has never revealed her actual name and the nickname is apparently based off the Jungle Book character Mowgli.

Sports.title: Journey to Wembley: After a fortnight of fretting over floodlights on the fritz, Nelson's FA Cup journey ends at Witton Albion - where home fans toasted victory with pina coladas!
Sports.content:
It’s the annual pina colada festival in the Witton area of Cheshire – the song about the drink, which topped the US charts in the late 1970s, was written by someone local to the place and they’ve spotted the commercial opportunity – so there are people walking around dressed as pineapples and wearing big yellow glasses on Saturday lunchtime. But life has not exactly been a cocktail party for Nelson, an East Lancashire ninth tier club, just lately.

They breeze through one of the challenges which faces them after arriving to face opponents one step above them in the pyramid. Their new yellow away kits for the season haven’t arrived and last season’s issue, which they’re still using, don’t have a No 18 jersey – needed today because you’re allowed seven subs in the FA Cup. Someone finds a white marker pen and inks the number on to a plain yellow away shirt. Wearing numbers on your back is mandatory in the tournament.

This is a minor obstacle compared with the floodlight problems which have been testing Nelson minds since we left them celebrating extra preliminary round victory at their ‘Little Wembley’ ground two weeks ago. That was the first part of our journey to Wembley told in 13 instalments, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

They’d signed off on a £30,000 contract, helped by FA grants, to replace the system of lights which had started to fail during evening games, only to find that the new ones still didn’t work.

The approved contractors didn’t seem to have mentioned that the cables and wiring supplying the lights also needed ripping out, and yet were sending the club legal letters demanding payment, as Nelson’s directors sought advice from the FA about the black hole they risked disappearing into.

Inside the home dressing room at the Bedspace Trust Community Stadium

Nelson captain Bill Priestley receives some treatment ahead of kick-off

A home steward - proudly sporting Witton Albion's colours - tucks into a pie at half-time

When we caught up with Nelson at their league away game at Charnock Richard in Lancashire, last Tuesday night, the floodlights were the prime topic of conversation as the players arrived in the car park. There had even been talk of a temporary ground move, which did not exactly delight the North West Counties League. Nelson’s proactive club sponsor Monks Contractors had offered supplying temporary structures.

In the end, they just went to work again. Volunteers helped dig two 100m trenches to lay the new cabling to the new lights and on Wednesday, they flicked the switch once more. ‘Let there be light?’ The look on Nelson director Rob Doherty’s face as the visiting contingent are welcomed into Witton’s snug little boardroom suggests so. ‘As of three days ago, they were working,’ he relates. The FA provided emergency funding.

Both these teams badly want to win this FA Cup Preliminary Round game. In his extremely modestly proportioned office Witton manager Benny Harrison, whose day job is a teacher at a special educational school, reflects at 2pm on the profound effects Marine experienced after playing Tottenham in the Third Round in 2021. The windfall helped win them two promotions in three years.

But as the rival teams’ executives gather in that boardroom, there’s a sense of mutual empathy about the existential threats which can be just around the corner for any non-league club.

‘There’s what goes on out on the pitch, and the fans and all that the lovely stuff,’ says Witton director Paul Sanderson, when Nelson relate their floodlight troubles. ‘And then there’s survivability stuff that fans don't know about. Trying to navigate things that can threaten your existence if you’re not prepared for anything.’

Nelson were on a precipice before new co-owners Stewart Fort and Chris Price arrived three years ago, invested and built up the team of volunteers who are their lifeblood. But Witton’s excellent little club museum, charting a 139-year history and signposted ‘probably the best non-League football museum in the world’, shows that they’ve also ridden football’s rollercoaster.

The museum chronicles the club’s journey to the 1992 FA Trophy final at Wembley, where they lost to Colchester. That period, which included a brief stay in the Conference, saw them splashing the surplus earned after selling their old ground to Sainsburys and building a new one, on players. The rewards were painful temporary. Witton struggled when the money ran out and the new stadium required major repair sooner than anticipated.

The sun’s out, though, and the FA Cup is blowing everyone’s troubles away. ‘Welcome to the best football competition in the world by a long chalk,’ states the stadium announcer. The appropriately named Witton groundsman James Spruce is reversing his mower out onto the excellent playing surface, his partner Katy Hulse is nursing a pina colada and her friend Barbara Bazley is watching the warm-up.

Groundsman James Spruce applies the finishing touches to the playing surface

Katy Hulse (left) enjoys a pina colada with her friend Barbara Bazley

Albion statistician Phil Chadwick has helped to curate one of the best club museum's in non-League

Nelson's 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader

‘When you make s*** decisions, it goes pear-shaped, so if someone makes a s*** decision, back them up and help sort it out,’ shouts assistant coach Liam Lishman, as he puts the squad through their paces. Thursday’s training session focussed on not allowing Freddie Garbutt, Witton’s towering 22-year-old striker, the chance to control and shoot.

At Charnock Richard, Nelson won 2-0, led by their own dangerous target man Sefton Gonzalez, who scored and hurled himself through his trademark somersault. Today, goalkeeper Chris Thompson is back after a bout of sciatica. There’s optimism in the air.

Against the backdrop of the chemical plants in salt-mining territory, Nelson discover what they’re up against in Garbutt and Witton’s attacking pace.

Nelson wing-back Darren Holden, outstanding in the previous round and at Charnock in midweek, is operating in his own half far more, protecting Nelson territory, yet removing one of the Lancashire team's attacking dimensions.

Jamie Edwards, Nelson’s force field, draws a sharp save and Gonzales has just headed a great opportunity into the ground when Witton’s Garbutt leaps to meet a corner and send his team ahead.

He’s one of only two players Witton have signed up to a contract, protecting his match fee if he’s injured and protecting the club if someone else tries to sign him, Witton chairman Graham Wood relates, back in the boardroom at half-time.

The winners today will collect £1,444 in prize money and that would be just as precious to Witton, a fan-owned club with 400 registered shareholders, none of them hugely wealthy, who are currently trying to make a community football facility.

Nelson players warm up at the side of the pitch before kick-off

Witton Albion play in the Northern Premier League Division One West, one division higher than Nelson

Visiting goalkeeper Chris Thompson keeps a Witton player at bay

Freddy Garbutt's first-half goal settled the game and sent Witton through to the next round of the FA Cup

Home boss Ben Harrison addresses his players at full time

‘That will bring us an income to put back into the club,’ says Wood, who has helped bring a commercial sponsorship deal with a locally based homelessness charity.

Nelson dominate a second half in which Holden is pushed forward more, encouraged by his wife Abi, who is live tweeting the match for the club’s website with another volunteer, Amy Holden, and taking photographs for next week’s match programme and the website.

In the main stand, 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes, which will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader, reflect the growing frustration. The ‘18’ inked onto sub James Hooper’s jersey is impressive. But it’s raining in Nelson hearts when the whistle blows and they tumble out of the competition.

Manager Arron Ripley stands in the sun-dappled centre circle ten minutes later and reflects on the way his ambitious side are evolving. ‘Last year we’d have kept launching it in a situation like that but we’re looking after the ball. We look like we’re enjoying it. We just weren’t clinical enough.’

Nelson can return fortified to their league campaign, confident, in so many ways, that the lights will stay on.

Sports.title: Newcastle edge closer to signing Nico Gonzalez from Man City - who want another midfielder after agreeing deal for Ayyoub Bouaddi: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period as clubs look to make big signings ahead of the new season. Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team... Gonzalez edges closer to Toon move Newcastle United are continuing to edge closer to agreement with Manchester City over a deal for Nico Gonzalez. Gonzalez is valued around £50million. The 24-year-old was an unused substitute in City’s win over Bournemouth on Sunday with Marc Guehi playing in midfield and it is clear that a move away may now be in his best interests. Nico Gonzalez is closing in on a move to Newcastle after falling out of favour at Man City Matthias Jaissle wants to add a midfielder with Premier League experience before the window closes. City agreed an £86m deal with Lille for midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi yesterday and want another before the window closes. Newcastle also admire Tottenham's Archie Gray though he has captained the side in pre-season and at the weekend in their 3-0 defeat to Brentford. Tigers target towering forward Hull are in talks for towering Union Berlin forward Ilyas Ansah. The Germany Under-21 international was considered for selection by Ghana ahead of the World Cup and Hull are offering £19m, including add-ons. The 21-year old is 6ft 6in tall and was a target for Besiktas earlier this year. He scored five goals and registered two assists in 26 games for Union Berlin last season. Hull had a £7m offer for Stoke City winger Sorba Thomas knocked back last week and are continuing to work on other options. Imps land Wheatley Manchester United striker Ethan Wheatley has joined Championship side Lincoln City. The 20-year-old agreed the move on Friday after seeing Everton pull out of a deal to sign him permanently earlier last week. Wheatley, who had a spell at Bradford last season, joins on loan for the rest of this campaign.
