World.title: Naro in Sicily becomes the latest Italian destination to offer homes for just €1
World.content:
What can €1 buy you? If you’re willing to swap your hometown for Sicily, it could get you onto the property ladder.

 

That’s because Naro, a medieval town on the southwest of the Mediterranean island, is offering would-be homeowners the chance to snap up a property for the price of an espresso.

Joining a growing list of Italian destinations with home listings at low prices, Naro, which is within the Agrigento province, is looking to breathe new life into the historic town while giving buyers the chance to restore abandoned buildings, tackle depopulation and bolster local tourism.

This initiative has been given the green light by the Comune di Naro local government authority and is open to both Italian and foreign nationals, provided they meet local requirements for purchasing and maintaining a property.

Applications can be submitted via the online Case 1 Euro Naro platform, which is available in multiple languages and walks interested buyers through the process of potentially landing a property.

According to the platform, buyers should consider investing because Naro offers a “historic centre with a strong identity, Baroque architecture, the Chiaramontano Castle, inland landscapes of Agrigento, and connections to Agrigento and the southern coast”.

And now for the €1 questions: Is there a catch? Well, yes – several, actually.

Typically, you get what you pay for, and for the cost of a cup of coffee, it’s no surprise that you won’t find a plush villa waiting for you in their catalogue.

When Euronews Travel browsed the listings, all the properties were listed as “needing to be renovated”, with one three-bed home overlooking the historic urban area, requiring inspection.

Beyond the €1 price tag, buyers are responsible for covering all associated notary fees, registration and cadastral taxes.

There’s also the matter of fixing the place up. Buyers must also cover the costs for project design of the property and ensuring it is safety compliant, adheres to landscape regulations and has undergone urban planning. And, there’s likely to be a deadline for getting all the work done.

Self-styled '€1 house buyer' George Laing snagged his third such property in June this year

Things to do in Naro, Sicily

Whether you’ve a spare €1 to invest in a property or are looking to travel off Italy’s beaten path, Naro is a striking inland town steeped in history, architecture and Sicilian charm.

Following a 2005 landslide, young artists worked on the façades of some of the neighbourhood’s ruined buildings, creating the MAN open air museum which you can wander through.

Naro has also preserved its Golden Gate, known locally as Porta d’Oro, which has a history that goes as far back as the 13th century. The ancient structure, featuring a pointed arch and stone battlements, was once part of a network of seven access gates that surrounded the city during medieval times.

As with other parts of Sicily, in Naro you can naturally snack on delicacies, including the native cassata – a Sicilian dessert of fluffy sponge cake, ricotta cream, chocolate chips – and pasta reale, which is a local sweet paste of finely ground almonds flavoured with vanilla, all adorned with candied fruits. The sweet treat traces its history to Arab-Palermo, with its name deriving from an Arabic term for large bowl where cream cheese filling was mixed with sugar.

Street food favourites, such as arancina, a morsel filled with fried rice, and cannoli can also easily be found in Naro, however, there are local varieties special to the town that can’t be found elsewhere.

World.title: European allies back Ukraine as country marks Independence Day without US envoys
World.content:
European leaders gathered in Kyiv on Monday as Ukraine marked 35 years of independence and its fifth Independence Day since Russia’s full-scale invasion — a milestone few expected when Russian forces advanced on the capital in February 2022.

 

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, on his first overseas trip since taking office, joined European Council President António Costa and other senior European officials in Kyiv for celebrations and talks with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The leaders are also meeting as part of the Coalition of the Willing, with French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz joining remotely.

Kyiv is pressing its allies for more air-defence missiles ahead of winter.

The European Union announced on Monday it would provide a fresh package of €6.1 billion in military assistance.

Speaking alongside Zelenskyy and the British prime minister António Costa paid tribute to the Ukrainian people for the “courage and bravery” that he said “inspire the world”.

“We will continue to provide as much support as necessary for as long as necessary,” he said, extending that commitment beyond the war to Ukraine’s future membership of the EU.

“International law must prevail. Russia will not prevail,” Costa said.

“The European Union cannot be neutral when international law is being violated. We are not neutral. We are Ukrainian supporters.”

Burnham compared Ukraine’s resistance against Russia to Britain’s fight against Nazi Germany, telling Ukrainians: “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st.”

He also pledged to help Kyiv strengthen its air defences ahead of winter.

UK Defence Minister Luke Pollard confirmed London will share technology with Ukraine to support domestic production of the long-range SCALP missile, saying: “We will stand with them for as long as it takes.”

Notably absent from Kyiv were senior representatives of the Trump administration.

Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner did not make the trip, despite speculation that Independence Day could bring their first visit to Ukraine.

Neither has travelled to Kyiv since taking a leading role in the US administration’s diplomatic efforts, despite repeated meetings with Russian officials and eight visits by Witkoff to Moscow.

Former US vice-president Mike Pence and Keith Kellogg, Trump’s former special envoy for Ukraine, did travel to Kyiv over the weekend and attended events surrounding the anniversary.

The price of independence

In a speech marking Independence Day, Zelenskyy told Ukrainians and international leaders that 35 years ago, intelligence agencies doubted Ukraine could survive as an independent state, suggesting it would fall back under Russian influence.

“But Ukrainians restored the independence of their state, and we will definitely protect the independence of Ukraine. No doubt about it,” he said, referring to Western intelligence assessments in the run-up to Russia’s full-scale invasion that Ukraine could fall within days or weeks.

When Russian forces advanced rapidly towards Kyiv in February 2022, few expected Ukraine to withstand the assault. Six months later, Ukraine marked its first Independence Day since the start of the full-scale war.

On Monday, it marked the occasion for the fifth time.

“Ukrainians will not be cobblestones under the feet of tsars and rulers. Ukrainians will not submit. Ukrainians will not be bargaining chips in disputes between capitals. Ukrainians will not submit to what they do not believe in. And they will definitely not abandon their own dream – the dream of living independently.”

commemorative ceremony marking Ukraine's 35th Independence Day outside St. Sofia cathedral in Kyivin Kyiv, Ukraine, Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. AP Photo

Monday’s commemorations also reflected the enormous cost of preserving independence.

Zelenskyy and First Lady Olena Zelenska began the day by honouring fallen defenders before the president presented some of Ukraine’s highest state awards to servicemen and women. Families of soldiers killed defending the country received honours awarded posthumously.

There was no traditional military parade through central Kyiv. Instead, Ukraine displayed domestically produced drones and other defence technologies that have become central to its war effort.

A dangerous moment in the war

The ceremony follows a severe escalation in Russian attacks on Ukraine.

Moscow has intensified ballistic missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, pushing civilian casualties to their highest levels since the opening months of the invasion and exposing Ukraine’s growing shortage of advanced interceptor missiles.

Zelenskyy said deliveries of Patriot interceptors had fallen significantly even as Russian missile attacks have increased.

Ukraine is seeking at least 300 additional interceptors ahead of winter, making air defence one of the central issues in Monday’s talks with its European allies.

World.title: Tens of thousands evacuated as Hawk wildfire nears western US city of Reno
World.content:
Authorities in Nevada urged tens of thousands of people to evacuate and ordered schools to remain closed on Monday as a fast-moving, wind-driven wildfire bore down on the western US city of Reno.

 

Around 42,000 people have been forced to evacuate and an additional 45,000 have been told to get ready to leave, Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve told CNN.

All but one school in Washoe County, where Reno is located, will remain closed on Monday, authorities said.

The Hawk Fire began on Saturday and had grown to 6,091 hectares by Sunday evening, showing "extreme fire behaviour," according to InciWeb, a US government website that tracks fire activity.

The fire was burning 8 kilometres northwest of Reno, a metropolitan area of over 280,000 people, according to census data from 2025.

No deaths have been reported, but at least six people have been injured, including three first responders, with several mountaintop houses destroyed, according to local media.

Officials said the fire was "human-caused," but did not say how it started.

A local fire rescue service said around 800 people were supporting firefighting efforts, including crews from Australia and New Zealand.

Pictures posted on X by the fire service showed flames and towering smoke clouds over mountains overlooking the city.

Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County.

The Hawk Fire "is spreading quickly and threatening homes and structures," his order said.

Local fire chief Richard Edwards urged people to be ready to evacuate immediately when told to do so.

Smoke billows in the distance as a wildfire burns in Reno, 23 August, 2026 AP Photo

"The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us as it's being driven by the winds. The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas," he said.

"If you have been told to evacuate, please don't wait!" Schieve, the Reno mayor, said in a statement on social media.

Reno is located in northwestern Nevada near the border with California and the tourist area of Lake Tahoe in the Sierra Nevada mountains.

World.title: Vaccine response: Scientists say the secret may already be in your blood
World.content:
Not everyone reacts to vaccines in the same way. Immune responses vary in strength depending on age, sex, prior illnesses and genetics.

 

In a new study, published in the Cell Press Blue journal, researchers at the United States National Cancer Institute’s SeroNet program investigated how pre-existing antibodies to common microbes can predict a person’s response to new vaccines.

“Certain biomarkers, when analyzed with AI, can predict who is likely to respond well to a vaccine, even before they receive it,” said Joshua LaBaer, who led the study, which suggests that some people may be more immune-ready than others.

Immunosuppression — having a weak immune system — is associated with a weaker antibody response to vaccination, which increases the risk of infection, disease severity and mortality.

The researchers found that, before receiving a vaccine, the body’s immune system already hints at how it will react and how robust the response will be.

The study analysed over 8,000 blood samples from more than 4,000 people, testing for antibodies against 185 antigens from common viruses, bacteria and autoimmune-linked targets.

Participants included healthy volunteers as well as people with weakened immune systems — due to conditions such as HIV, multiple myeloma and solid organ transplantation — all of whom received the COVID-19 vaccine.

The researchers then used artificial intelligence to analyse patterns in samples collected before and after COVID-19 vaccination, identifying antibody signatures that helped categorise patients as either strong or poor vaccine responders.

They identified what they call "sentinel antibodies," which act as indicators of a person’s likely immune response to a given vaccine, helping predict how an individual’s body will react to the virus.

“We identified universal antimicrobial signatures that were positively associated with the top 25% of high COVID-19 vaccine responders,” the researchers noted.

The study found that higher levels of certain pre-existing antibodies, especially those against common organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and human parainfluenza virus 3 (HPIV-3), were associated with stronger COVID-19 vaccine responses.

Transforming vaccination strategies

By using pre-existing antimicrobial antibody profiles as predictive biomarkers, clinicians could identify individuals likely to develop a weak immune response before they are immunised.

The study applied machine learning to construct predictive models to classify individuals with suboptimal vaccine response.

“Predicting which individuals will mount poor antibody responses before vaccination could improve personalised vaccination strategies,” the researchers wrote.

This would allow for targeted interventions such as tailored dosing schedules, different vaccine types or additional booster requirements for those at higher risk.

World.title: Shein launches IPO at a sharply lower valuation — and Europe is central to its success
World.content:
The Chinese-founded online retailer launched its Hong Kong share offering on Monday and expects trading to begin on 1 September. It is seeking to raise as much as $1.77 billion (€1.5 billion).

 

Shein said it would use the proceeds to strengthen its technology, brand and international operations. That includes hiring more local sales and marketing staff in major markets such as Europe, although the prospectus does not allocate a specific amount to its European expansion.

According to Shein’s filing, the company plans to offer nearly 280 million shares at a price between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50. The offer price is expected to be agreed by 28 August and formally announced on 31 August, before the planned market debut the following day.

The flotation follows several years of attempts to list in New York and London. Shein, which was founded in China but is now headquartered in Singapore, secured approval from Chinese regulators in July to pursue the Hong Kong listing.

In the meantime, the company’s valuation has dropped sharply.

“Shein’s peak valuation was approximately $100 billion in 2022, supported by its unique position in the global retail market,” Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said before the latest announcement.

Shein’s rapid growth was driven partly by its success in marketing inexpensive, trend-led clothing on social media, particularly TikTok. That strategy proved especially effective during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The company reported a full-year net profit of $2.06 billion in 2025 but swung to a $99 million quarterly loss in the first three months of 2026.

The reversal followed the United States’ removal of its customs exemption for low-value parcels, although Shein said an accounting charge also contributed to the loss.

Why Europe matters to Shein

Europe is central to Shein’s business. The European Union and the United Kingdom generated $14.8 billion (€12.7bn) in revenue in 2025, equivalent to 35.4% of global revenue. It was Shein’s largest disclosed regional market.

Shein had an average of approximately 156 million monthly users in the EU between August 2025 and January 2026, putting it among the continent’s largest online marketplaces. The figure includes visitors who did not make a purchase.

Europe is therefore both crucial to Shein’s growth and one of its greatest risks. The company must either absorb the new costs or raise prices, potentially weakening the main advantage that helped it attract customers.

Given the region’s size, even a relatively small fall in sales or profit margins could have a significant effect on Shein’s global performance.

And new EU customs charges and regulatory investigations pose serious risks to the company’s low-price model.

The EU abolished its €150 customs-duty exemption for low-value consignments on 1 July. An interim duty of €3 now applies to each distinct product category within an affected parcel, while an additional EU-wide handling fee is expected later in 2026.

Shein operates 18 warehouses in Europe, but its supply chain remains heavily dependent on China: more than 90% of its global revenue in 2025 came from products stored in its central Chinese warehouses.

The prospectus says Shein expects to respond to the EU changes by raising some prices, holding more inventory locally, expanding local fulfilment and strengthening trade compliance.

“There might be a short-term adverse impact on our sales volume in Europe as we increase prices to offset a portion of the increased costs, while the long-term impact remains too early to fully assess.”

This presents Shein with a difficult balance. Higher prices could protect its margins, but may weaken the rock-bottom pricing that has been one of the brand’s main competitive advantages.

Shein opened its first permanent physical store at the BHV Marais department store in Paris on 5 November 2025, after previously relying on temporary pop-up shops. The opening underlined the importance of France to the company, while also provoking opposition from politicians, trade groups and established fashion brands.

Shein plans to spend approximately 40% of the net IPO proceeds — around HK$5.25 billion (€570 million) — on marketing and strengthening its global presence over the next four years.

This will include digital advertising, major brand campaigns and an expansion of local sales and marketing teams. Europe is identified as a major market, but Shein does not say how much of this budget will be spent in the region.

Legal battles in Europe

Shein's European presence has been increasingly overshadowed by critics, accusing the company of labour abuses, excessive environmental damage and intellectual-property infringement.

Shein told AFP previously that it has “zero tolerance” for forced labour, commissions independent audits of suppliers and requires them to comply with its labour standards. It also argues that its production model “dramatically reduces waste”.

Shein has also been accused repeatedly of intellectual property infringement, disclosing in July that it was facing more than 40 related lawsuits.

Another hurdle arose in February of this year, when the European Commission launched an investigation into the firm's compliance with the Digital Services Act.

This is examiningShein’s controls against illegal products, potentially addictive platform design and the transparency of its recommendation systems. A finding of non-compliance could expose the company to a fine of up to 6% of its annual worldwide turnover, as well as orders to change how its platform operates.

Separately, France has adopted legislation aiming to reduce the environmental impact of the textile industry.

The law restricts advertising for ultra-fast-fashion companies and introduces environmental penalties of up to €12 per item in 2026, rising to €20 from 2030. The measures are due to take effect on 1 September.

French authorities have also imposed penalties totalling more than €210 million on Shein since 2025, including environmental and consumer protection claims.

Investing in Shein

Unlike SpaceX, which reserved an unusually large part of its June flotation for individual investors, Shein is not running a public offer for ordinary European retail investors. Its prospectus states that no public offering has been authorised outside Hong Kong, while the international tranche is principally directed at institutional and professional investors.

European retail investors may nevertheless be able to buy Shein shares after trading begins, provided their broker offers access to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

Speaking of Shein's recent financial performance,Coatsworth said that "even though Shein makes billions of dollars on an annual basis, the trend is negative". The company's net profit fell from $3.4bn (€2.9bn) in 2024 to $2bn (€1.7bn) in 2025, before it made a $99 million net loss in the first quarter of 2026. “Net revenue growth has slowed in recent years and margins have been squeezed,” the analyst added.

“To make matters worse, Chinese rival Temu has emerged as a major challenger to Shein and eaten some of its lunch. The Iran war has also negatively impacted Shein as it has hit demand, pushed up costs, and caused delivery delays to certain markets,” Coatsworth said.

According to the analyst, Shein's potential future growth could be driven by the company's data-led production system and ability to react quickly to changing consumer tastes.

“The bull case is that Shein has considerable scale and agility, meaning it can bring new designs to market quickly and get a clear idea what’s working and what’s not,” Coatsworth said.

Shein says it can restock popular products in as little as five days and had 281 million active customers at the end of March 2026.

Its marketplace, allowing third-party merchants and brands to sell directly to customers, could also provide a route into more product categories and geographical markets.

However, lower valuation could provide an opportunity to those with risk appetite. “A cut-price valuation might present an opportunity for contrarian investors who believe the potential rewards outweigh the long list of risks,” Coatsworth said.

World.title: Dolly Parton shares health update and considers ‘avatar performances’ in future
World.content:
Country icon Dolly Parton has shared a health update with her fans amid ongoing health issues and the death of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, who died last March.

 

Parton has been open about her grief and the impact of Dean’s death on her mental health, sharing that she has felt “worn down and worn out”.

The music legend, now 80, has been forced to pull out of a string of recent appearances due to ongoing issues.

“I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl,” she told People. “It’s not like I haven’t been through hard times with my health,” she said, noting that in the early ’80s she was “down for several months with female issues”.

“But I think because we live in a 24/7 world with social media, everything gets magnified in ways it wasn’t years ago. I used to joke that I was the Queen of the Tabloids, but now I guess I can say I’m the Queen of Social Media AI!”

She added: “Seriously, though, even though I’m still healin’, I’m still workin’.”

Parton also told the outlet that she was working alongside various companies to create “avatar performances” in order to bring fans new experiences.

She did not expand any further, as the discussions are still in the “early stages of development”.

Should Parton go down the avatar route, she would join several artists who have used the digital technology, which has allowed artists both living and dead to craft lucrative shows and tours.

Dolly Parton performs during an event celebrating the Missouri statewide expansion of Dolly Parton's Imagination Library - 27 August 2024 AP Photo

From Michael Jackson, Elvis and Tupac Shakur to Gorillaz and ABBA, hologram concerts are a growing trend. They feature "Pepper’s ghost" forms of performers – named after the illusion technique created by the English scientist John Henry Pepper.

Pepper popularised the effect during a 1862 Christmas Eve theatrical production of Charles Dickens’ “The Haunted Man and the Ghost’s Bargain”. The illusion was a hit and was then used in carnival sideshows, cinemas and amusement parks.

The first time it was used for concerts was in 2006 for the Grammy Awards, when Pepper’s ghost technique was employed to project Madonna with the virtual band members Gorillaz onto the stage. Since then, several acts have used the technology, with the most elaborate being the ongoing concert attraction ABBA Voyage, which uses Pepper’s ghost combined with digital projection and motion-capture technology.

Even politicians have taken to using the technology, with Narenda Modi projected at 88 locations across India in 2014 and then-French Presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélanchon giving a speech in 2017 at a campaign event in Aubervilliers he wasn’t physically at.

Recently, it was announced that an AI avatar of Ozzy Osbourne was in the works. However, this was met with backlash from fans who described the stunt as a “cash grab” and a “heresy” - criticism to which the rocker’s widow Sharon Osbourne responded...

She told critics she “doesn’t need your fucking money” and that the Prince of Darkness would have been supportive of the project.

“For somebody to turn around to me and say I’m doing a cash grab? No, you don’t know my husband, OK? I know my husband,” she said. “My husband would say to me over and over, ‘After I go, how long do you think I’ll be remembered?’”

Dolly Parton’s health update comes after she rerecorded her 1977 hit song ‘Light of a Clear Blue Morning’ earlier this year alongside fellow artists Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, Queen Latifah and Reba McEntire. The single was released to raise money for pediatric cancer research at the Monroe Carell Jr. Children’s Hospital at Vanderbilt in Nashville, Tennessee.

The news also follows an academic poll in the US, which found that Parton tops the list of the most beloved public figures in America.

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.title: Myanmar: Why Rohingya refugees can't return
World.content:
Nine years after the Rohingya were driven from Myanmar, claims of progress on refugee returns have revived talk of repatriation.

Myanmar's military-backed government is again talking about bringing Rohingya refugees home from refugee camps in neighboring Bangladesh.

Earlier this month, authorities in Naypyidaw, Myanmar's capital, said they had made progress verifying Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh for possible repatriation.

Of the 820,000 names submitted by Bangladesh, Myanmar said it had verified around 308,000 as former residents but would not repatriate them until security conditions improve in civil war-torn Rakhine State.

But analysts told DW that large-scale, safe repatriation is now arguably further out of reach than at any point since 2017. Myanmar is engulfed in civil war, the military no longer controls most of Rakhine state, and the Rohingya remain denied citizenship.

How Myanmar's Rohingya were driven from their homes

In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched sweeping operations in northern Rakhine state after alleged attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) militant group on security posts.

More than 1 million Rohingya have been crammed into the camps in southeastern Bangladesh, the world's largest refugee settlement Image: AFP

More than 750,000 Rohingya, a long-persecuted Muslim ethnic minority in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, fled to Bangladesh, joining hundreds of thousands displaced by earlier crackdowns.

Muslim-majority Bangladesh now hosts around 1.2 million Rohingya refugees, mostly in camps around the southern coastal district of Cox's Bazar, according to UN bodies.

Myanmar does not recognize the Rohingya as one of its 135 officially recognized ethnic groups and has long referred to them as "Bengalis," implying they are migrants from Bangladesh despite generations of Rohingya having lived in Rakhine.

UN investigators found evidence of genocidal intent by Myanmar's military, while the United States argued in 2022 that members of the military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya.

A genocide case brought by the West African nation of Gambia against Myanmar remains before the International Court of Justice in The Hague.

Myanmar's 2021 coup triggered a nationwide civil war that is still raging, even after a much-criticized election earlier this year saw the formation of a civilian government, which remains dominated by officials from the military and junta.

"Safe repatriation is simply not possible," Ronan Lee, a researcher at Loughborough University and author of the 2021 book "Myanmar's Rohingya Genocide," told DW.

There is a civil war in Myanmar and the economy has collapsed, Lee said, meaning a return under present conditions would carry a high risk of the Rohingya again facing violence from the military.

"Myanmar's government is dominated by the same military that genocidally deported the Rohingya in 2017," Lee added. "Life in Myanmar today would be more dangerous for the Rohingya than when they were forcibly deported in 2017."

Safe return 'simply not possible'

Moe Thuzar, head of the Myanmar Studies Program at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, agreed that repatriation is much less realistic today than at any point since 2017.

Even if Myanmar's military-backed authorities wanted to facilitate returns, which few analysts think they do, they no longer control most of Rakhine, Thuzar noted.

The Rakhine-based ethnic Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group distinct from the Rohingya insurgent group ARSA, now controls much of the state, including northern areas from which many Rohingya fled.

Rohingya caught in the middle of Myanmar's civil war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UN reporting has documented serious abuses against Rohingya by both the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, including restrictions on movement, arbitrary detention and forced recruitment.

Antje Missbach, professor of global and transnational migration and mobility at Bielefeld University in Germany, told DW that even if a voluntary return policy could be agreed, Myanmar's government has not offered the Rohingya citizenship.

Many Rohingya villages have also been destroyed, while others are now occupied by different communities, she added.

"Rakhine is not safe," she said, noting that hundreds of thousands of Rohingya are estimated to have left Myanmar for Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh over the past two years.

Camp crisis changes refugee behavior

Yet if returning to Myanmar looks increasingly unrealistic, remaining indefinitely in Bangladesh is also becoming more difficult. Funding shortages, worsening insecurity and a lack of opportunities to work or study are putting new pressure on the camps.

"The worsening conditions in Bangladesh's Rohingya camps are fundamentally altering refugee behavior, pushing a population already traumatized by genocide into increasingly desperate and precarious survival strategies," Rafiqul Islam, a professor of peace and conflict studies at the University of Dhaka, told DW.

"The camps, which host nearly 1 million refugees, are facing a perfect storm of crisis: severe overcrowding, chronic underfunding, food ration cuts, limited educational and livelihood opportunities, and growing security concerns," he added.

There has been an increase in Rohingya refugees trying to make dangerous sea voyages to Malaysia, Indonesia, or other Southeast Asian countries, while gang violence and other criminal activity are on the rise, Islam said.

There is also a growing trend of child marriage, child labor, and school dropout rates, "as families struggling with food insecurity are forced to make impossible choices between education and survival, sacrificing their children's futures for immediate needs," Islam added.

Bangladesh: Could the UN help the Rohingya return home? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Food insecurity is now universal across the camps, according to the World Food Programme. UNICEF reported last year that admissions of Rohingya children for treatment of severe acute malnutrition had risen 27% year-on-year.

Mizanur Rahman, an anthropologist at Jagannath University in Dhaka, told DW that Bangladesh has legitimate concerns about bearing the burden of such a large displaced population, so the answer cannot simply be to ask Dhaka to do more. "There needs to be genuine international burden-sharing," Rahman said.

The UN and Bangladesh say $710 million (€608 million) is needed in 2026 for the most urgent refugee and host-community needs, of which around 60% has been funded.

The EU has allocated €23.4 million in humanitarian funding for Bangladesh this year, most of it supporting Rohingya refugees and host communities, and separately announced a €14 million development grant through UNHCR in June.

While the Rohingya remain unable to build permanent lives in Bangladesh, the conditions for a safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar appear to have moved further out of reach.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: US to unveil new Iran sanctions, says war entering 'endgame'
World.content:
In what Donald Trump has called "economic D-Day," the US says the new economic sanctions will be "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled." Tehran says any support of the measures is an "act of war."

The US is preparing to unveil a raft of new economic measures targeting Iran and its trade partners amid the stalled six-month-old war in the Middle East.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce the measures in a press conference at 1800 GMT on Monday.

Iran, a country that has already been living under international sanctions for decades, has vowed to retaliate.

In a post on X, Bessent described the sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary."

He said US President Donald Trump had "dismantled Iran's military capabilities," destroyed nearly 100% of its military factories and "buried its nuclear program."

"We are now entering the endgame," he added.

'Economic D-Day'

Last week, Trump announced what he called an "economic D-Day" for Tehran, threatening harsher sanctions targeting not only Iran but also countries that continue to do business with it.

"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent said.

Already last week, the United Arab Emirates, one of Iran's largest trading partners and its biggest source of imports, announced that it was suspending all trade with Iran.

It was not clear if the US measures will include action against China, Russia and India.

Ahead of Monday's press conference, China's Foreign Ministry said Beijing was monitoring developments closely and would do what is necessary to protect its rights. The ministry also added that sanctions and pressure tactics do not help resolve problems.

How has Iran responded to the new sanctions?

Over the weekend, the head of Iran's top security body warned that Tehran would see any country's support of the US measures as an "act of war."

Supreme National Security Council leader Mohsen Rezaei said Iran would "retaliate in a seismic manner" to the sanctions by targeting other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf.

"If the economic war ​continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said.

The current situation in the Iran war

The Middle East war began on February 28 when Israel and the US carried out strikes on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Tehran responded with strikes on energy infrastructure and US bases in the Gulf region.

While the two sides have stopped the bombing, talks to end the conflict have stalled, with control over the Strait of Hormuz remaining a key sticking point. Iran has effectively closed the waterway, crucial for global oil and gas shipments, while the US maintains a blockade of Iranian ports.

Under a memorandum of understanding signed in June, the two sides had 60 days to negotiate an end to the war and reach an agreement on Iran's nuclear program. But that period expired last week with no signs of a deal.

Meanwhile, Pakistan's army chief was expected to travel to Iran on Monday as part of efforts to revive diplomatic talks in the conflict.

And on Tuesday, Oman's foreign minister is set to meet his Iranian counterpart to continue talks on the Strait of Hormuz.

Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter: 50 years on stage
World.content:
Anne-Sophie Mutter constantly reinvents herself. For her 50th onstage anniversary, the star violinist is surprising audiences with sounds from around the world and never-before-recorded commissions.

The list of international composers who have written for star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter is a long one. It features names like Krzysztof Penderecki and Sofia Gubaidulina, along with Andre Previn and Jörg Widmann. In recent years, women like Iranian-Dutch composer Aftab Darvishi and South Korean composer Unsuk Chin have also written works for Mutter.

On the occasion of the violinist's 50th stage anniversary, she's now recorded over 30 works either dedicated to her or commissioned by her — all part of her "ASM Forte Forward" project on the Alpha Classics label.

Anne-Sophie Mutter is deeply committed to social causes Image: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

The first album in the series, "East Meets West," reflects not just the artist's musical passions but also her social engagement. The opening "Likoo for Solo Violin," composed by Aftab Darvishi for Mutter in 2024, leaves a powerful impression. "Likoo" is a lament about loss, written at a time when especially women in Iran were fighting repression by the regime.

Giving women a voice

"I wanted to create a musical tribute to the people in Iran and to those fighting for freedom, coexistence, empathy and equality, in the hope that these atrocities would never be repeated," Mutter told DW. "War is raging on our wonderful planet even as I'm playing, but I won't give up hope for love and empathy." Mutter's performance of it is deeply moving — one can almost hear the women's cries in the violin, fading into silence.

With the situation in Iran deteriorating, Mutter says it's especially important to her to keep "Likoo" in her repertoire. "I have great admiration for Persian culture and for the female composers who still live in Iran — such as Golfam Khayam, who managed to send me her score by email during a pause in the shelling. I still hear from her from time to time," Mutter says.

"These female composers in Iran fascinate me, and the piece 'Likoo' in particular. That's why — also sadly because of the current situation — it's very important to me to perform 'Likoo' at the anniversary concert." The concert is being held on August 25 at the Lucerne Festival.

Her 1976 stage debut in Lucerne

On August 23, 1976, a 13-year-old Anne-Sophie Mutter took the stage at a young artists' concert in Lucerne. It was there that conductor Herbert von Karajan first encountered the young talent. A year later, he hired her for a concert with the Berlin Philharmonic at the Salzburg Easter Festival. So began Mutter's long collaboration with Karajan and his Berlin orchestra.

Anne-Sophie Mutter at the International Music Festival in Lucerne in September 1976 Image: ZUMA/Keystone/IMAGO

Another figure who shaped her musical life on stage in the 1980s was Swiss conductor and patron Paul Sacher. "He was a major influence on my interest in contemporary music," Mutter says. She cherishes the undogmatic learning experience she gained from Sacher and her other mentors. Sacher always afforded her the freedom to decide how she would approach an assignment. He passed a motto on to her: "What I can't do, I can learn. What I can't learn today, I can learn later."

The Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation

A four-time Grammy winner and recipient of Japan's Praemium Imperiale, she's now supporting highly gifted young musicians through the Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation. She encourages her scholarship recipients to embrace social engagement alongside contemporary music. She's herself a supporter of humanitarian organizations such as Save the Children and Doctors Without Borders, and from 2021 to 2025 served as German Cancer Aid's chairwoman.

In 2019, Mutter received the Praemium Imperiale, sometimes referred to as the Nobel Prize of the arts. On the right is Klaus-Dieter Lehmann, the prize's representative for Germany Image: Jörg Carstensen/dpa/picture alliance

It's difficult for young musicians to build an audience and make money with contemporary music, Mutter says. "All the same, I want to keep them grounded and show them it's not just about getting rich and famous; they have a role to play in society — in social environments. Playing at a nursing home, for example, or teaching, supporting charitable organizations with benefit concerts."

A platform for composers

As well, Mutter uses the work she commissions — including from former and current scholarship recipients — to help advance their careers. "I want to give these pieces a platform, along with a recorded presence. Without that, these wonderful works couldn't be heard all over the world."

The next album in the "ASM Forte Forward" series being released for the anniversary is "American Tunes #1." It includes works by Andre Previn, whom Mutter was married to for four years, as well as US composer Sebastian Currier, who has written several pieces for Mutter.

Fellows from the Mutter's Virtuosi ensemble accompany her on international performances Image: JANEK SKARZYNSKI/AFP

"It gives me particular pleasure that many works by colleagues from my foundation, as well as by former and current scholarship recipients, have actually been recorded," Mutter says. "I have managed to put many of my young musicians at the center of this new 'Forte Forward' series, and that makes me very happy."

Albums of memories

To further mark her onstage milestone, Mutter has planned several projects with her longtime label, Deutsche Grammophon. Among them is the release of seven location-centered albums featuring selected works — pieces that, as in the case of the city of Lucerne, were premiered there or hold special significance in Mutter's musical life.

So far, "My Berlin," "My London" and, in connection with the anniversary concert in Lucerne, "My Lucerne" have been released digitally. The seven planned albums will follow the artist around the globe, from Berlin, London and Lucerne to Tokyo and New York.

As early as age 17, Anne-Sophie Mutter was playing a Stradivarius violin Image: Karl Staedele/dpa/picture alliance

Anne-Sophie Mutter's constant companion is her Stradivarius violin. "The violin is the coolest instrument in the universe. For 50 years I've tried again and again to show that," she says.

The instrument is her voice, too, she adds: "I find it fascinating how music becomes so expressive precisely where language ends, and how in this cosmos of creativity we can connect, discover ourselves, give ourselves over to expression, and truly experience life."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Syria sentences Assad-era top Muslim cleric to life in prison
World.content:
Muslim cleric Ahmad Hassoun was convicted of crimes including inciting sectarian violence and justifying murder. He is the latest Syrian official aligned with ousted President Bashar Assad to face trial.

A Syrian court on Monday handed a life sentence to Ahmad Hassoun, the country's former grand mufti under ex-President Bashar Assad.

The religious cleric, who vocally supported the regime's policies, was found guilty of a raft of crimes including inciting sectarian unrest and justifying murder.

Judge Fakhreddine al-Aryan said the official religious establishment under Assad had "justified the use of barrel bombs that targeted civilian areas and caused widespread destruction, which constitutes a violation of the rules of international humanitarian law."

A string of trials over civil war

Hassoun is the 10th Assad-era figure to be sentenced under Syria's new authorities.

Earlier this month, Assad himself and his brother Maher were sentenced to death in absentia for atrocities committed during Syria's civil war.

More than half a million people were killed and millions were displaced during the war, which began in 2011 following a crackdown on anti-government protesters. It ended in December 2024 with Assad's ouster in an offensive by Islamist-led militants.

The former president fled Syria as his regime fell and is believed to be in Russia.

Assad tried in absentia as Syria charges ex-regime members To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rights groups raise concerns

Death sentences have also been handed to Bashar's cousins, Atif Najib and Wassim al-Assad, who were tried in person.

The sentences have been welcomed by Syrians who had previously criticized the new government for not moving fast enough to act against Assad-era officials. But human rights groups have voiced concerns that the trials are being rushed and may not be fair.

"Advancing justice for the litany of serious crimes committed in Syria requires more than just convictions, but building a system that can deliver competent, impartial, and independent justice," said Balkees Jarrah, the Middle East and North Africa director for Human Rights Watch.

Back to Yarmouk: A Syrian family rebuilds and seeks justice To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is Ahmad Hassoun?

Hassoun, 77, held the position of Syria's top Islamic cleric from 2005 until 2021, when the position was abolished.

An Aleppo native, he was known for his close ties to Assad and was often seen at his side on religious occasions.

He was arrested at Damascus Airport in March last year while trying to flee the country.

Syrians still wait for rebuilding one year after Assad To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Dutch pull out of 'no longer neutral' Eurovision
World.content:
The Netherlands will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria, the state broadcaster has said, citing divisions over the situation in Gaza. It's the second time the country is boycotting the event.

Dutch state broadcaster Avrotros said on Monday that the Netherlands will not be taking part in next year's Eurovision Song Contest (ESC).

The event can "no longer be considered neutral," given the war in Gaza, it said.

Eurovision boycotts

This year, the Netherlands was joined by Spain, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia in staging the biggest political boycott in Eurovision history in protest at Israel's participation. Hundreds of pro-Palestinian protesters also marched outside the event.

Avrotros Director-General Taco Zimmerman said international conflicts were increasingly affecting the contest and "undermining its neutral character," adding that it had "become a platform for division."



Four nations boycott Eurovision over Israel inclusion To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier this month, ESC organizers announced new rules that bar any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

"However, the recently announced ‌changes ... do not provide sufficient confidence that ​the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest ⁠has ​been restored," Avrotros ​said.

The pop spectacle is watched by tens of millions of viewers around the world each year.

Israel came close to winning the competition in 2025 and 2026, placing second in both events.

The 2027 ESC will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria, after singer Dara won this year's competition in Vienna, Austria.

Dara from Bulgaria won this year's Eurovision with the song 'Bangaranga' Image: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP

The Netherlands and Eurovision: 'Very close to our hearts'

The Netherlands took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest in 1956.

They have won it five times since then, most recently in 2019 with Duncan Laurence and his song "Arcade."

According to the Eurovision website, it was the first competition entry to reach 1 billion streams on Spotify.

The country's withdrawal from the next Eurovision is "painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year," Zimmerman said.

"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts," he added.
