World.title: How will the Law and Justice split affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively. Radical-right challengers At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party. Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support. Responding to declining support At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance. Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank. The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values. In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction. Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment. However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church. Although they were also critical of Brussels overreach, Morawiecki’s faction preferred to avoid escalating conflict with the EU and argued that PiS had to broaden its appeal to younger, urban, more centrist-conservative Poles who found radical cultural rhetoric off-putting. Programmatic differences and personal ambitions The conflict became so destabilising because, although rooted in genuine programmatic and strategic disagreements, personalities and individual ambitions also played a major role. While Kaczyński maintained formal control of the party, his advancing age escalated debates over PiS’s direction and leadership, and these tensions intensified after the party failed to translate its presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki’s surprise summer 2025 election victory into broader momentum. For his part, Morawiecki grew increasingly impatient and frustrated as hardliners sidelined him, while his supporters were afraid that they would be excluded from PiS candidate lists at the next election. These long-simmering tensions came to a head in April, when Morawiecki announced the formation of Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a think tank-like platform focused on economic development The association was widely interpreted by Kaczyński and PiS hardliners as a direct challenge to party unity and the leader’s authority. The leadership ruled that Development Plus violated the PiS statute, which explicitly prohibits members from joining political organisations that conflict with the party’s goals. While Morawiecki insisted that it was simply a modest intra-party policy forum, by registering an organisation with dozens of parliamentarians, he gave his faction a formal institutional shell that could potentially act as a launchpad for his own rival breakaway party. Initially, Kaczyński and Morawiecki came to a compromise agreement whereby Development Plus would work within an official party expert group. However, in July the situation escalated when the PiS leadership issued an ultimatum banning members from participating in internal political factions (clearly targeting Development Plus) and instructing parliamentarians to sign loyalty declarations confirming that they were not involved in any such groupings. Most complied, but 40 parliamentarians affiliated with Development Plus refused to do so, accusing the leadership of political blackmail. Ultimately, Kaczyński announced that, by refusing to sign, Morawiecki and his allies had effectively left the party, while Development Plus framed it as expulsion over policy differences caused by “plotters” surrounding the party leader. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 An even more fragmented right The loss of 40 deputies means that PiS is no longer the largest parliamentary caucus, thus losing procedural advantages, committee control and visibility. The departing group includes many experienced and talented politicians, particularly in the economic and foreign policy fields. The split also reduces PiS’s funding, staffing, and in some regions local organisation, as well as creating the risk of demoralisation and further defections. Even if the Polish right secures a parliamentary majority at the next election, PiS’s relative influence could be greatly reduced. Although Kaczyński’s formal party leadership remains unquestioned, the split signals to the broader right that his authority is waning and undermines his claim to be the undisputed hegemon and central broker on the right; he is increasingly now one leader among several. It also further erodes the model that Kaczyński has built over many years as the main ideologue and ultimate arbiter of internal PiS factions. In earlier crises, this personal authority and control gave him leverage to keep everyone on board so that disagreements were managed internally, and even disillusioned figures usually stayed in, or returned to, the party. Indeed, by adding a fourth distinctive player, the PiS split further compounds the divisions on the Polish right that have deepened since the last election, transforming what was once a relatively consolidated “big tent” bloc into a multi-polar competitive field. For sure, polls conducted after the split show the combined right-wing vote as competitive overall, but even if this level of support remains stable, or even increases slightly, it is now divided across more options. This is significant because Poland’s proportional electoral system uses the d’Hondt counting system that favours larger groupings. It also creates the risk that smaller right-wing parties such as Morawiecki’s new grouping could fall below the 5% parliamentary representation threshold, so their votes are excluded from seat allocation. All of this makes it harder for the right to translate raw voter support into political power. Moreover, even if the right-wing parties win a combined parliamentary majority, post-election coordination becomes much more complex with four (or more) actors whose leaders’ rivalries, different priorities and historical animosities complicate forming a stable coalition government. Nawrocki’s role will be crucial In the light of this, Nawrocki has emerged as a critical unifier with crossover appeal across the fractured Polish right. His presidential election victory showed that he could attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists and consolidate a broad right-wing coalition, including the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. As president, he operates outside direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative unifying figure on the right, which gives him much greater moral and symbolic stature than a partisan leader immersed in day-to-day machinations. Nawrocki has also used his constitutional powers and standing, including a legislative veto that the government lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, to position himself assertively as a powerful counterweight to the Tusk administration, and is currently Poland’s most popular politician. Nonetheless, Nawrocki’s potential to act as a possible right-wing unifier and broker is limited. For sure, he can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 However, Nawrocki has no formal unifying mandate and his success ultimately depends on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Without broader cooperation, even his efforts will only mitigate, not eliminate, the damage from a divided right, and personal and ideological rivalries currently run deep and cannot be easily overridden. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally above the fray and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, he also lacks the control over party organisational machinery needed to micro-manage and enforce messy backroom deals. Pivotal but not transformative? Initial polling conducted since the split suggests that Morawiecki’s new grouping would likely clear the 5% threshold and enter parliament with a small-to-medium-sized fraction; according to Politico Europe, it is currently averaging around 6% support. Although this could make it a pivotal player in coalition talks, it does not suggest that the grouping can dramatically reshape the country’s political landscape. Moreover, its support appears to be drawn mainly from PiS’s traditional electoral base, so it is simply further fragmenting the existing right-wing vote rather than drawing in a significant number of new voters who hitherto supported the governing coalition parties. For sure, Morawiecki‘s project has advantages that many newcomers lack, notably its leader’s very high name recognition and a sizeable bloc of high-profile, political heavyweight allies, much larger than any previous PiS breakaway faction. His grouping immediately became the third largest parliamentary fraction, giving it visibility, funding, and organisational backbone. However, although there are some rare exceptions that usually involve major figures with significant resources breaking from established parties, it is a familiar pattern in post-1989 Polish politics for a brand new “startup” party to show an early bounce, benefiting from initial media coverage, only to fade or disappear as voters drift back to more established groupings or abstain at the next election. Sustaining momentum requires local organisational infrastructure, reliable funding, rapid professionalisation, and a clear identity, which new parties often lack. Indeed, to be successful a new startup should really attract at least 10% support initially simply because of its “newness”. Over the years, PiS breakaway politicians have established new parties that either quickly disappeared from the political scene or were eventually reintegrated into the grouping. Temporary relief for Tusk From a short-term tactical perspective, the PiS split is a welcome political gift for the Tusk government, shifting the media focus away from criticisms of its record and recent scandals and controversies. It has for example, blunted the opposition’s ability to maintain a sustained assault over a scandal involving high earnings for, and mismanagement by, a KO-connected doctor, alleged VIP access and potential patient harm at the Warsaw South Hospital, which had previously dominated the summer news headlines. The ruling coalition is likely to survive until next year's election, but its prospects are hampered by a weak domestic record, writes @AleksSzczerbiak The government has therefore made security key to its reelection narrative, but that also carries risks https://t.co/w2UeNaTwAO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 1, 2026 However, the PiS split has not resolved the deeper image and performance problems that have dragged down the Tusk government’s approval ratings. The administration struggles with perceptions of slow delivery on promises while facing a hostile president, and if these problems persist, or new controversies reignite strongly once the PiS drama cools, the government will very quickly find itself back on the defensive. The PiS split only provides temporary relief; to win the next election, the ruling coalition needs to improve its own standing, not rely on opposition mistakes. World.title: Polish NGOs urge PM’s “right-hand man” to withdraw constitutional court candidacy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A group of Polish civil society organisations has urged a former government minister to withdraw his candidacy to become a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, saying his close ties to the prime minister could undermine confidence in the court’s independence. In a joint statement, the nine organisations say that restoring the legitimacy of the court, which has been in crisis since 2015 following illegitimate judicial appointments made by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, requires not only addressing legal irregularities but also rebuilding public trust. “The existence of the Constitutional Tribunal as an organ of judicial power only makes sense if it is an independent arbiter,” they say. 🔴Wspólnie z innymi organizacjami apelujemy do dr. M. Berka o rezygnację z kandydowania do TK, a do Sejmu o wybór osoby niezależnej politycznie. Droga do praworządności to nie „odbijanie” Trybunału, ale odbudowa jego autorytetu. Przeczytajcie nasz apel, link w komentarzu ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/LPlbk39lNr — Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) August 20, 2026 The appeal follows Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s announcement that Maciej Berek, who until recently served as a government minister and whom Tusk has described as his “right-hand man”, would be put forward as a candidate for the Constitutional Tribunal. The choice has drawn particular attention because Tusk came to power promising to “depoliticise” the court after the previous PiS government appointed former politicians as judges. “Regardless of the extent to which the tribunal has become politicised, the way to reform this institution cannot be for it to be ‘recaptured’ or ‘taken over’ by another ruling majority,” the NGOs write in the statement. The organisations, including the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Institute of Public Affairs and the Stefan Batory Foundation, say Berek’s close ties to the current political leadership could cause his appointment to be perceived as political, regardless of his legal qualifications or personal integrity. “Not only must courts and tribunals operate independently and impartially, but citizens must also recognise and have confidence in that independence and impartiality. This is not possible when judges are appointed whose links to the government are immediately apparent,” the organisations add. “We therefore call on Dr Maciej Berek to withdraw his candidacy in the interests of the independence of the constitutional judiciary.” The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 The organisations also argue that Berek’s nomination goes against a principle that the current ruling coalition sought to introduce: that anyone who has held political office within the previous four years should be barred from appointment to the tribunal. Berek was a government minister until last week. The coalition’s proposal was included in a bill approved by parliament in 2024. However, the Constitutional Tribunal itself later ruled the provision unconstitutional after former President Andrzej Duda, an ally of PiS, referred the legislation for review. “Although this law has not come into force, it would be reasonable for the Sejm to adhere to the standard it has adopted,” they said, referring to the lower chamber of the parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 However, the selection of Berek, whose candidacy was put forward by MPs from Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has exposed divisions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from centre-right to left. “We were supposed to be different from PiS; we were supposed to do things differently, not exactly the same way,” Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, told Polsat News. Paweł Śliz, leader of the centre-right Poland 2050’s (Polska 2050) caucus, said Berek would make an excellent Constitutional Tribunal judge were it not for his recent role as a government minister. “I consider him an excellent, outstanding professional; I value his experience and expertise. However, my position on this matter is unequivocal. I will not compromise my principles,” he told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition opposing Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. Last week, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz told PAP on Thursday that “there are serious doubts” about Berek’s formal qualifications to become a Constitutional Tribunal judge. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland summons Israeli ambassador over discontinued investigation into killing of Gaza aid workers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) have discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. “Partnership requires mutual respect,” declared foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for [the] IDF’s excessive use of force[,] are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.” Partnership requires mutual respect. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. https://t.co/9H0nhiDE4H — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 20, 2026 The incident in question took place in April 2024, when Israeli drones struck a convoy delivering humanitarian aid from World Central Kitchen (WCK), a major international food relief NGO. The attack killed seven aid workers, including Soból. The incident caused outrage in Poland, whose government demanded that Israel fully explain the circumstances. The IDF expressed “sincere sorrow” over the deaths and pledged to carry out a “thorough and transparent” investigation. On Wednesday this week, the IDF announced that it had closed the case after determining “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”. The IDF said that its troops had identified a gunman on one of the trucks in the convoy. It also claimed that WCK had hired an armed security force to protect the convoy without coordinating that with IDF authorities and that the convoy deviated from the route previously agreed with the IDF. However, the IDF also acknowledged that it had mistakenly identified several individuals as being armed. It added that attempts to contact WCK representatives over a half-hour period while the convoy was on the move were unsuccessful. The IDF noted that, after the incident, two military officers were removed from their positions while three others were reprimanded. But it found that there was no basis for any further action. ⚖️ IDF prosecution rules on five FFAM cases: The IDF says its General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism has completed reviews of approximately 150 exceptional wartime incidents since the beginning of the war and transferred them to the Military Prosecution. Decisions… pic.twitter.com/H5g4qOu5e2 — Israel Realtime (@IsraelRealtime) August 19, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying that it was “greatly disappointed to receive the information provided about the discontinuation of the proceedings by the Israeli military authorities”. It announced that it had summoned the Israeli ambassador in order to “communicate a critical assessment of the actions taken to date to clarify the causes and course of the tragedy”. It also noted that Polish prosecutors are still conducting their own investigation and that the foreign ministry had informed the Israeli ambassador that they “expect the Israeli side will provide the relevant Polish authorities with all necessary explanations and materials requested”. “The circumstances of the tragedy should be fully investigated and [we] do not accept that the perpetrators are avoiding legal and moral responsibility,” concluded the ministry, adding that “the families deserve adequate compensation”. We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024. And we fundamentally disagree with their decision about criminal investigations into the IDF airstrikes that killed our team. Read our full statement here:… — World Central Kitchen (@WCKitchen) August 19, 2026 The IDF’s findings were also condemned by WCK itself, which called them “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. It added that, “at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody”. The NGO repeated its demand for an independent investigation into the incident, “because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct”. On Friday, the UK, Canada and Australia, whose citizens were also killed in the strike, issued a joint statement calling the IDF’s decision to drop the investigation “shameful” and another example of the lack of accountability for incidents in Gaza. Joint statement from the foreign ministries of Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom on Israel closing the investigation into strikes on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza on 1 April 2024 ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/V3CZe286tN — Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (@FCDOGovUK) August 21, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: New official tasked with promoting Poland criticised over error-strewn, potentially AI-generated report
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing errors and which shows signs of being generated by artificial intelligence. The document mislocated major Polish cities and included bizarre language mixing Polish and English. It was marked as being part of a project financed by the sport and tourism ministry, though the ministry itself has denied that claim. The opposition has called on prosecutors to investigate potential misuse of public funds. ⁉️ Czy “Markę Polska” ma nam wygenerować sztuczna inteligencja? ⁉️ Czy Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki zapłaciło 200 000 złotych w ramach zadania publicznego za raport wygenerowany przez AI? ⁉️ Czy mogę prosić Panią Minister prof. @b_mroz_gorgon o odniesienie się do tych pytań… pic.twitter.com/lM2AY88oAh — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 The official in question, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, is a professor at Wrocław University of Economics who was appointed three weeks ago as the government’s plenipotentiary for the promotion of Poland’s brand, a newly created position. She was presented at a press conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. However, this week, journalists and commentators began highlighting cases of bizarre errors from a report, titled A Self-Portrait of the Poles (Polaków Portret Własny), published last year with Mróz-Gorgoń named as the author, in her position as president of a think tank called Marka Polska (Brand Poland). The report contained some glaring errors, such as describing the city of Katowice as being in “north central” Poland (whereas in fact it is in the south) and Wrocław as being in the “northwest” (when it is actually in the southwest). Geografia – czyli gdzie leżą Katowice A propos miast jest też ciekawy chochlik lub też, jakby to powiedział ktoś złośliwy, klasyczna halucynacja AI. Przy opisie badań FGI miasta opisane są w następujący sposób (zdjęcie poniżej): 👉 Olsztyn – północny wschód 👉 Szczecin -… pic.twitter.com/SF6XBRfhWS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 Other parts contain strange analysis, such as noting that “after World War Two, Germany did not build its brand on the Holocaust”. The text also features unusual language, including random use of words in English, some of which have been turned into Polish ones. It is also regularly features words written in capital letters. One sentence, for example, refers to “INSTABILNOŚĆ” and “REZILIENCE”, presumably meaning “instability” and “resilience”, but neither of which is a Polish word. Another section claims that 95% of Poles born after 1990 are “polilingwalni” (an invented Polonised version of “polylingual”) who speak “angielski fluent”, a strange linguistic mix that means they speak English fluently. As well as the unusual language, the very claim that 95% of young Poles speak fluent English, as well as that many additionally speak Mandarin, has been questioned by many commentators. The report also contains bizarre errors in footnotes, which are numbered randomly (on one page, three consecutive footnotes are numbered “41, 517, 6”) and some of which are completely empty. A number of expert commentators have suggested that the text contains clear indications that it was generated by AI, a claim supported by evidence from programmes that check texts for AI-generated content. AI czy nie AI, oto jest pytanie Czytając ten raport kilkukrotnie, trudno mi było pozbyć się wrażenia, że nikt poważny, a szczególnie naukowiec z tytułem doktora habilitowanego, nie wygenerowałby dużych części raportu, za który zapłacili podatnicy, w jakimś LLM. No bo przecież… pic.twitter.com/jyTexgmeXS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 As well as bearing Mróz-Gorgoń’s name as author, the report also features on its front cover the logo of the sport and tourism ministry. The first page then includes a note saying that the project was carried out under an initiative co-financed by the ministry. After the issue began to draw attention and criticism on Thursday, the ministry issued a statement saying that the report was not ordered by them, was not part of any agreement to which the ministry was a party, and that no request to use the ministry’s logo was submitted. However, a social media post last November by deputy sport and tourism minister Piotr Borys shows him attending an event to present the report. He thanked Mróz-Gorgoń for coordinating the project and inviting him to the presentation. 📚W Akademii Leona Koźmińskiego odbyła się prezentacja raportu „Polaków Portret Własny”, przygotowanego Think Tank Marka Polska. To wyjątkowe wydarzenie poświęcone premierze badań dotyczących DNA Marki Polska. 🧬To pierwsze tak kompleksowe badanie, które pokazuje, kim jesteśmy… pic.twitter.com/jb7KdCJTPM — Piotr Borys (@piotr_borys) November 26, 2025 On Thursday evening, Mróz-Gorgoń herself addressed the controversy in an interview with Polsat News. She said that the report was actually a “work in progress” that “should never have appeared in the public space”. However, she still defended the work, saying that “the research was conducted reliably” and “the conclusions stand up to scrutiny”. But she also admitted that the writing of the report had been “aided by artificial intelligence”. In separate remarks to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), she said that “we used AI tools solely for transcription, summarising and text editing; they did not design research content or draw conclusions…We worked according to social science methodology, diligently and without cutting corners”. Meanwhile, on the Marka Polska think tank’s website, where the report had been published, it was initially changed on Thursday to being marked as a “draft version” before later being deleted entirely. Od raportu i deklaracji, że “praca badawcza [została] przeprowadzona zgodnie z zasadami nauk społecznych, rzetelnie i merytorycznie, w oparciu o opisaną metodologię”, przez “work in progress”, aż do “Oops! That page can’t be found”. Myślę, że to słowo “Oops!” jest najlepszym… pic.twitter.com/OaSTxkwKwa — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 On Thursday evening, the main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), announced that it was submitting requests to both prosecutors and the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (ABW) to investigate the use of around 200,000 zloty (€46,380) in state funds for the project that the report was allegedly part of. PiS has also called on Mróz-Gorgoń to resign or to be fired. On Friday, a deputy digital affairs minister, Dariusz Standerski, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that “all the circumstances surrounding the creation of this report will be clarified”. The controversy around Mróz-Gorgoń comes just days after the sport and tourism ministry was involved in the launch of a new advertising campaign designed to encourage tourism to Poland, but which many commentators have argued was poorly conceived and executed. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A speed of 253 km/h (157 mph) has been reached by a Pendolino train during tests carried out as part of preparations to speed up rail connections between Poland’s major cities from next year. The plans will see the journey time between Warsaw and Kraków cut to well under two hours. “Polish rail is accelerating – and 250 km/h is just the beginning,” declared the infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak, alluding to plans for Poland to later begin running trains at speeds of up to 320 km/h. Osiągnęliśmy 250 km/h na Centralnej Magistrali Kolejowej❗🚅 Dzisiejsze nocne testy systemu GSM-R na linii nr 4 zakończyły się pełnym sukcesem. Oznacza to, że pociągi pojadą tą trasą z rozkładową prędkością 250 km/h już w przyszłym roku❗ Pozwoli to znacznie skrócić czas… pic.twitter.com/ndXvePZP4t — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) August 18, 2026 The tests on the GSM-R data transmission system, a communication standard designed to be used at very high speeds, were carried out on Monday night. Trains will be able to run on Poland’s Central Main Line (CMK), which connects Warsaw with Kraków and Katowice, at a scheduled speed of 250 km/h from December 2027. That will cut the expected journey time between Warsaw and Kraków, the country’s two largest cities, by around half an hour to 1 hour and 52 minutes, reports rail news service Portal Kolejowy. It will also be possible to travel from the capital to Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, in around three hours. The fastest current connection is 3 hours and 30 minutes. Reaching the target speed of 250 km/h was a “very important moment for Polish rail”, said Maciej Kaczorek, a board member of PKP Polskie Linie Kolejowe, the state railway infrastructure manager, quoted by news website Money.pl. Poland has been operating Pendolinos, built by France’s Alstom, since 2014. The trains are designed to run at speeds of up to 250 km/h, but currently operate at a maximum of 200 km/h in Poland and run on routes connecting Warsaw, Kraków, Wrocław and the Tricity area. However, this week’s tests are not a record rail speed in Poland. In 2013, a Pendolino reached 293 km/h during a test on the CMK a year before the high-speed trains commenced passenger services in the country. A Polish Pendolino high-speed train has begun running in the Czech Republic for the first time. The Prague-Bohumín service will run until June as part of a certification process that Polish operator PKP Intercity hopes will lead to a Warsaw-Prague route https://t.co/hmUNd7ft0E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 Speaking to Rynek Kolejowy, deputy infrastructure minister Piotr Malepszak said that it had “taken too long” for the network to be adapted to allow regular speeds of 250 km/h. The current government, which took power in December 2023, has much broader plans for expanding high-speed rail travel in Poland, including building 2,700 km of tracks capable of carrying trains at 320 km/h. In December 2025, state rail operator PKP Intercity launched a tender for 20 such trains. They would cut the journey time between Warsaw and Gdańsk, on Poland’s Baltic coast, to around 100 minutes – from 2 hours 25 minutes currently – by 2040, Malepszak told the Polish Press Agency in June. Passenger numbers on Poland’s rail network have been booming in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. Poland has launched a tender to buy 20 trains that can reach speeds of 320 km/h (199 mph), making them the fastest ever to travel on Polish tracks. Currently, Poland's fastest trains, Pendolinos, can reach maximum speeds of 200 km/h https://t.co/XcGdJJggkx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish government proposes middle-class tax cuts funded by increased rates for wealthiest
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has unveiled plans to reduce income tax rates for an estimated 3.5 million people earning around or slightly above average salaries. The costs of the cuts would be covered by increasing the tax rate for large companies and individuals with the highest earnings. The changes, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk says are intended to “provide relief and assistance to the growing middle class”, would come into effect from next year – when the government is facing re-election. World.title: A Multi-Brand K-Beauty Pop-Up Is Coming to Prague This September
World.content:
A Korean beauty pop-up will bring eight K-beauty brands and K-pop entertainment to Prague’s Vltava River this September.

The HARUNARU K-Beauty Pop-up will take place aboard KVASOUL, a self-brewing boat restaurant, from September 4 to 8.



An industry preview for beauty professionals and influencers will be held on September 3.

Visitors will be able to discover, test and buy products from eight Korean brands, including GASH, ranked No. 1 at Olive Young, South Korea’s leading beauty retailer, and ilso, known for its pore-care products.

The event will also feature K-pop performances, a Random Dance Challenge, an idol-style makeup show and a dedicated selection of K-pop albums and merchandise.

The pop-up is aimed at introducing emerging Korean beauty brands to consumers and industry professionals in the Czech Republic and across Central and Eastern Europe.

Entry is free, although visitors are encouraged to register online in advance.

The event is organized by Bramasole Prague s.r.o., which operates several Korean restaurant brands in Prague.

HARUNARU K-Beauty Pop-up

📍 KVASOUL, Vltava River, Prague

📅 September 4–8, 2026

World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

1:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

1:05 p.m. – Street dance class

1:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

2:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:00 p.m. – Hat Jazz performance

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

6:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

7:00 p.m. – Acrobatic performance

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Bolt Launches App-Free Ride Kiosks in the Czech Republic
World.content:
Bolt has introduced self-service kiosks in the Czech Republic that allow customers to order a ride without a smartphone, mobile data or the Bolt app.

The first kiosk is now operating at Westfield Chodov in Prague. A second will open at Westfield Černý Most on September 1. The company says it plans to consider other high-traffic locations in the future.



The kiosks use TapBox technology and provide access to the same Bolt driver network, pricing and safety standards available through the app.

Customers can place an order directly at the screen, making the service available to people who do not use smartphones or cannot access their phones at the time.

Both shopping centres have also introduced dedicated parking spaces for Bolt drivers collecting passengers. Customers are directed to these designated areas rather than having to meet drivers at potentially unsafe stopping points such as bus stops.

How Bolt kiosks work

Ordering a ride takes several steps. Customers enter their destination, select a ride category and provide their phone number. The available categories are Standard, Comfort, Premium and XL.

Payment is made by card. Once the booking is completed, the kiosk prints a confirmation and sends an SMS containing the vehicle details, estimated arrival time and instructions for finding the driver.

The kiosks operate around the clock and support Czech, English, German, French and Ukrainian.

Each ride booked through a kiosk carries an additional CZK 25 fee.

Bolt says the system could also benefit drivers by connecting them with customers who might otherwise be unable to use the app. The company expects the kiosks to reduce waiting times between rides at busy shopping centres and create additional opportunities for drivers.

The Czech launch follows the introduction of similar kiosks in Slovakia earlier this summer, including at airports.

World.title: Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Cycle Routes but Cycling Numbers Barely Rise
World.content:
Prague is continuing to expand its cycling infrastructure, but the number of recorded bicycle journeys across the city has remained largely unchanged.

Automatic counters installed on major cycling routes recorded about 5.6 million passages in 2025, roughly 1 percent fewer than the previous year.

After adjusting for counter failures and temporary route closures, however, the Technical Road Administration (TSK) calculated a 0.4 percent increase in cycling traffic.



Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Routes Away From Traffic

The city added 18 kilometers of two-way cycle paths and other cycling routes separated from motor traffic during the year. The total length of marked cycling routes increased by one kilometer to approximately 550 kilometers.

Routes separated from car traffic now account for 263 kilometers of the network, an increase of seven kilometers compared with the previous year.

TSK operates automatic counters at 31 locations on Prague’s main cycling routes. The devices use induction loops or radar to record cyclists and can determine their direction of travel.

The largest increase in two-way cycling routes came over the past year. Their combined length grew from 63 to 81 kilometers. These routes allow cyclists to travel in both directions on streets that are otherwise one-way for motor vehicles.

New two-way routes were added mainly in Prague 7 around Letná, in Prague 5 in Barrandov, and in Prague 6 around Na Petynce, Rozdělovská and Podbaba.

Modřany Remains Prague’s Busiest Cycling Route

The highest number of cyclists was recorded in Modřany, at the intersection of Vltavanů and U Kino streets. The counter registered 578,016 passages during the year.

Another 540,656 cycling journeys were recorded on Povltavská Street south of Troja Castle.

The largest year-on-year increase was recorded on the Barrandov Bridge, where cycling traffic rose following the completion of its more than two-year reconstruction.

World.title: “Upcycling” Prague: Old Offices and Industrial Sites Find New Life as Apartments
World.content:
Former offices, commercial properties and industrial sites in Prague are being converted into apartments rather than demolished, giving developers another option in a city struggling to build enough new homes.

The approach is sometimes described as “upcycling” — adapting ageing buildings for a new purpose while making use of structures and land that are already developed.

One recent example is in Pankrác, near Vyšehrad, where an office building has been converted into the Mo-cha HOME residential complex.



Developed by Cimex, the project opened this spring with 91 fully equipped apartments, most of them in the Czech 2+kk layout, consisting of a living room with a kitchenette and one separate bedroom.

Existing buildings offer valuable locations

Owners of older properties increasingly have to decide whether to renovate them, change their use or demolish them. Many were built for different needs and standards than those expected from buildings today.

Their locations, however, can be a major advantage. Older properties are often close to public transport, shops and other services, making them attractive for residential conversion.

Transforming an existing building can also be faster to prepare than developing a completely new project on a brownfield, although each property must be assessed individually.

The approach can preserve existing structures, reduce demolition and make better use of land that is already developed.

More former offices are becoming homes

Pankrác is not the only part of Prague where old buildings are being converted into housing.

In Holešovice, the former Tesla complex, once used for light-bulb production, has been transformed into a residential project with 149 apartments. The building had stood unused for years, but its main structure remained in relatively good condition.

In Prague 7, another former administrative building near Urania has also been adapted for residential use.

In Prague 3, PSN is preparing the reconstruction of a former telecommunications exchange on Fibichova Street. Built in 1926 and designed by architect Bohumír Kozák, the building is expected to become a rental housing project with 116 units.

One of the largest transformations is planned in Žižkov, where the functionalist former General Pension Institute will be converted into an apartment building with smaller units. The project received a building permit last year.

Not every older building is suitable for conversion. Technical condition, layout, location, project costs and future use all determine whether redevelopment makes economic and practical sense.

World.title: More Czech Companies Test Four-Day Work Weeks Despite Political Resistance
World.content:
A growing number of companies in the Czech Republic are experimenting with a four-day working week, with some reporting higher productivity and greater employee satisfaction.

But politicians remain reluctant to make the arrangement a standard option across the country.

Under the model, employees work four days instead of five while keeping their full salaries. Companies that have introduced the system say workers can maintain their output while having more time to rest.



At Trinity Group, the arrangement has been in place for five years. Jan Hanulík, the company’s product and marketing director, said productivity had risen despite employees working one day less each week.

“Although we have one working day less, productivity has increased,” Hanulík said, adding that the company’s results have roughly doubled since the system was introduced.

A survey cited in the report found that around 70 percent of employees in the Czech Republic would welcome a four-day working week.

Politicians remain cautious

The idea has already been adopted in different forms elsewhere in Europe. In Belgium, for example, employees can request to work their weekly hours over four days rather than five. The system therefore does not necessarily mean fewer working hours.

Czech politicians, however, argue that a single system would not work across all sectors.

Labor and Social Affairs Minister Aleš Juchelka of ANO said a legally mandated four-day week could create problems in areas already facing staff shortages, including social services and health care.

SPD lawmaker Lucie Šafránková also said the working week should reflect the conditions of individual professions and employers rather than follow one nationwide rule.

Czech companies are already experimenting

Several companies have introduced or tested four-day schedules, including SAB Finance, Phonexia, Sherpas, Digiskills and Café Eternity.

Not every experiment has lasted. The Cognito agency eventually returned to a traditional five-day working week after testing the shorter schedule.

World.title: Foreign Workers Now Make Up 22% of Czech Employees
World.content:
Foreign workers accounted for around 22% of all employees in the Czech Republic at the end of 2025, according to data from the Czech National Bank (ČNB).

Their number has nearly tripled over the past decade, rising from about 323,000 in 2015 to 935,000 last year.

The increase has significantly changed the makeup of the Czech labor market. Foreign workers represented roughly 8% of all employees in 2015. By the end of 2025, their share had reached 22%.

Ukrainians made up the largest group of foreign employees, with approximately 358,000 working in Czechia at the end of last year. Slovaks were the second-largest group, numbering almost 230,000.



The Czech labor market has also seen increasing numbers of workers from other countries outside the European Union, including the Philippines and India.

Foreign workers are particularly important in several sectors, including manufacturing, construction, retail, transport and hospitality.

Their presence is most pronounced in accommodation, food services and hospitality. Foreign nationals accounted for more than half of all employees in the sector at the end of 2025.

The figures should, however, be interpreted with some caution when comparing individual industries. The CNB notes that employment agencies can distort the sectoral breakdown.

Workers employed through agencies are recorded in official statistics under administrative and support services, even when their actual jobs are in manufacturing, construction, logistics or other industries.

World.title: Tesco Teams Up With Wolt. Can Express Delivery Save Its Czech Business?
World.content:
Tesco will launch a new express delivery service in Prague in September, working with Wolt to deliver orders within 40 minutes.

The service, called Tesco Hned, will initially be available from selected Tesco stores in the Czech capital.

The launch comes as speculation continues over a possible sale of Tesco’s Central European operations and the British retailer’s future in the Czech Republic.



Tesco Hned is designed for customers who need groceries and other everyday products quickly rather than as part of a larger planned shop. Orders will include food, drinks, cosmetics, household products, pet supplies and other goods.

The company says its standard online shopping service will continue to focus on larger orders, while the new option is aimed at customers who need a few items immediately.

Tesco has already tested the service at six Prague stores. It plans to extend Tesco Hned to another 22 locations in the coming weeks.

Delivery will be provided through Wolt, giving customers access to Tesco products through the courier company’s platform.

Tesco faces questions over its future

The new service comes at a difficult time for Tesco in Central Europe.

According to the Financial Times, Tesco’s British owners are considering selling their operations in the region, including the Czech Republic. The Schwarz Group, which owns Lidl and Kaufland, and Polish retailer Biedronka have reportedly been mentioned among potential buyers.

Tesco has not announced plans to leave the Czech market, and the launch of Tesco Hned suggests the company continues to invest in its services.

World.title: Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ
World.content:
Lower new-build property prices in Bucharest and Poland’s major cities may catch the attention of Hungarian buyers, but the success of a property investment abroad is determined by much more than the purchase price and achievable rental income. An analysis by Cordia comparing the Hungarian, Polish and Romanian markets, while also looking at Spain, examines the differences, costs and yields investors should consider when thinking about entering a new-build market in the region or buying a newly built home in a popular holiday destination.

By the end of the first quarter of this year, the average price per square metre of new-build homes in Budapest had risen above HUF 1.9 million, 8% higher than in March 2025. Against this backdrop, Bucharest may look particularly attractive: even using the average exchange rates recorded during the first quarter, the gross average price remained below HUF 1.3 million per square metre despite annual price growth of more than 10%.

Among Poland’s major property markets – Warsaw, Kraków, the Tricity area (Sopot, Gdańsk and Gdynia), Wrocław, Poznań and Łódź – the capital is the most expensive. By the end of March, the average price per square metre of new-build homes in Warsaw, calculated in forints and referring to properties in shell-and-core condition, approached HUF 1.7 million. In Poznań, meanwhile, the average remained below HUF 1.2 million. These figures are among the findings of a regional market comparison prepared by Cordia, one of Hungary’s leading residential property developers.

“These potentially significant price differences may also spark the interest of Hungarian investors. For our projects abroad, we naturally assist buyers who are considering purchasing a new-build apartment either in regional markets or even on the Spanish Riviera,” said Áron Görög, Sales Director at Cordia.

“On the Costa del Sol, where we are now developing our second project, we are seeing significant appreciation. The average price of €7,220 per square metre recorded in March this year – equivalent to around HUF 2.6 million – was almost 9% higher than a year earlier. It is also important to note that developers there traditionally advertise net prices, to which 10% VAT is then added.”

If you missed it: Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

What about rental prices?

For a property investment, achievable rental income and the characteristics of the local rental market are also crucial.

In Poland, for example, lower prices per square metre come with unit rental prices comparable to or higher than the Budapest average. As a result, gross rental yields calculated in euros range between 4.5% and 6%, even after taking into account the additional costs required to bring a property to a fully finished, move-in-ready condition.

It is also worth looking at the differences between individual Polish cities. Poznań, for instance, is a major industrial and logistics hub, with low unemployment and more moderate new-build property prices. In Warsaw, on the other hand, investors can expect relatively high property prices but also stable rental demand, as the capital is the country’s main business centre.

In Bucharest, relatively low new-build prices compared with other regional markets offer an attractive entry point. However, gross rental yields are also broadly in line with the Polish average, at around 5–6%.

“Sales have recently begun at Cordia’s latest Bucharest project, the 274-apartment Centropolitan development. We are seeing significant interest in the project from buyers in Hungary as well,” the expert said.

Double land costs and shell-and-core apartments in Warsaw

It is also worth examining what lies behind the significant differences in property prices across the region.

When interpreting Warsaw’s prices, it is important to bear in mind that, unlike in Hungary and Romania, developers traditionally offer apartments in shell-and-core rather than fully finished condition. This means buyers face substantial additional costs beyond the purchase price before they can move in.

At the same time, construction costs for an average Warsaw or Bucharest development are 25–33% lower than in Budapest. Land prices, however, tell a different story. In Warsaw, land represents a cost more than twice as high in the per-square-metre price of a property compared with the Hungarian or Romanian capital.

Differences in tax systems must also be taken into account. In Hungary, the standard VAT rate for new-build homes is currently 5%, and VAT can also be reclaimed in the case of homes in designated brownfield regeneration zones. In Poland, an 8% VAT rate applies to residential properties smaller than 150 square metres, while the portion above that threshold is subject to a 23% rate. In Romania, following a temporary period with a lower tax burden, the standard VAT rate returned to 21% in August this year.

“Alongside differences on the cost side, prices are also strongly influenced by the complexity of administration, the varying strength of demand and the range of government measures available to support buyers,” Görög emphasised.

Air conditioning is now a basic requirement in Bucharest and Budapest

“The technology used in the buildings we develop is fundamentally similar. There is also no difference in the fact that we build apartments with terraces everywhere, although this is less important to Polish buyers. Efficient floor plans are expected across all markets, but environmental awareness and energy efficiency are less prominent considerations in Poland and Romania.

“As summers become increasingly hot, buyers in both Budapest and Bucharest are placing greater emphasis on effective cooling systems, whereas this is not as common in Poland, particularly in the northern parts of the country,” the expert said.

Interestingly, Poland is introducing energy-efficiency ratings for multi-apartment buildings only this year, making it the last EU member state to do so. Experts believe this could encourage investors to sell older, energy-inefficient apartments and instead seek out newly built, energy-efficient properties.

According to Cordia’s experience, however, there is one common trend across all markets: buyers everywhere are increasingly demanding higher quality, better-equipped homes and additional services, such as communal spaces and facilities, co-working areas, lounges and gastro bars.

Here, the company can draw particularly strongly on its experience in the more developed Spanish market. This gives Cordia a competitive advantage in markets such as Romania, where such extras are still relatively uncommon in projects developed by other companies.

World.title: Two light aircraft collide and crash in Austria, killing both pilots
World.content:
Two light aircraft collided and crashed near Krems Airport in Lower Austria on Monday morning, killing both pilots, according to local police.

Two aircraft caught fire after collision

The accident happened near Krems Airport, with the two aircraft catching fire after the collision. Initial information indicates that neither aircraft was carrying anyone other than its pilot, according to Kronen Zeitung.

Both pilots died in the accident.

The exact circumstances of the crash are not yet clear.

One aircraft was towing a glider

According to the Krems volunteer fire brigade, the aircraft involved were two ultralight planes. One of them had been towing a glider when the collision occurred.

The glider had already detached from the towing aircraft shortly before the accident. The pilot of the aircraft then turned, after which the two ultralight planes collided.

The glider itself was not involved in the crash.

Police and emergency services are investigating the circumstances surrounding the fatal collision.

World.title: Orbán’s secret EU campaign revealed: How Hungary took its message to Europe – and how much we paid for it
World.content:
A newly obtained media plan reveals that Viktor Orbán’s government paid more than HUF 313 million for a campaign placing the Hungarian prime minister’s seven-point criticism of the European Union in newspapers across Europe in 2021.

Hungarian taxpayers paid more than HUF 313 million for a government advertising campaign that promoted then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s criticism of the European Union in foreign newspapers, newly obtained documents reveal.

The campaign, launched in the summer of 2021, was considerably broader than previously known. While two full-page s – one in a Danish newspaper and another in Spain – attracted attention at the time, documents obtained by investigative outlet Átlátszó show that Orbán’s message was ultimately published in 18 foreign newspapers.

The campaign came at a particularly tense moment in Hungary’s relationship with the EU, following a series of disputes over the Hungarian government’s policies and its increasingly confrontational stance towards Brussels.

A HUF 313 million campaign against the “European empire”

The , titled On the Future of the European Union – Hungary’s Proposals, presented seven points under Orbán’s signature. Its opening message declared: “We say no to a European empire!”

According to the media plans obtained from the Prime Minister’s Cabinet Office, the government paid a total of HUF 313 million gross for the campaign. The net advertising cost was HUF 213.4 million. On top of this came a 15 per cent agency fee of HUF 32 million paid to New Land Media, the company responsible for organising the campaign, followed by VAT.

The documents indicate that the government initially targeted even more publications. In total, 25 newspapers appear to have been approached, although seven ultimately did not publish the . One of them, Bulgaria’s 24 Chasa, reportedly could not run it because of technical reasons. The campaign therefore went far beyond the two s that became publicly known at the time.
