World.title: From Film Sets to Prompts: The AI Short-Drama Revolution
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018927/From Film Sets to Prompts: The AI Short-Drama Revolution
World.content:
China’s booming ultra-short drama industry is being reshaped by the rapid rise of AI-generated video. In Zhengzhou, one of the country’s major production hubs, directors, actors, crews, and film bases that once fueled the industry’s explosive growth are now facing shrinking budgets, fewer shoots, and an uncertain future. Meanwhile, in other cities like Wuxi, AI studios are embracing the same technology to produce dramas faster and at a fraction of the traditional cost. As the two worlds increasingly converge, the question is no longer whether AI will change filmmaking, but what role humans will have in it.

Additional reporting: He Qitong; story editors: Apurva and Qi Ya; video editor: Lü Xiao

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018928/Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.title: Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018928/Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.content:
“We bought three tickets,” a teenager says to a woman asking to use the empty seat beside her — occupied by snacks — her sister sitting on the other side.

“We’re all in the same carriage,” the standing woman says. “Shouldn’t we help each other out?” She calls a train attendant for help.

“Places 5, 6, and 7 — those seats are theirs,” the attendant says after checking the teens’ tickets. “You need to talk to them about it. Telling me won’t help.”

This scene, which took place Aug. 18 on a slow train traveling from Shanghai to the southwestern city of Chengdu — a 27-hour journey — was captured in a video that went viral in China this past week.

Online, people heatedly discussed whether the girls should have shared the seat or whether they were entitled to keep it for themselves. The topic rose to the second-highest place on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list, receiving over 37 million views and 12,000 discussions as of Monday.

Many were in support of the girls’ decision, arguing that giving up their seats would be a favor, not an obligation, as the teens themselves had paid for the three tickets. Others said that they were “wasting public resources.”

Still others contended that the train attendants should have been more proactive, pointing to railway ticketing rules that say customers can only buy one ticket for themselves per train and that if the ticket holder does not board, their seat should be reassigned by train attendants.

Despite these stipulations, passengers can buy tickets for others using their identification information on train ticket purchasing platforms.

The girls’ mother did just that, buying their tickets as well as entering her own information for the third seat, according to a now-deleted post she made on Aug. 20 on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

“My original intention was to keep them from taking up other people’s space because they had too much luggage, so I bought an extra ticket,” she wrote. “Since they’re both girls and didn’t want to sit with others, I bought three tickets together.”

In response to the issue, 12306 — China’s official train ticketing and service platform — told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper that in the event that a passenger does not board the train, their ticket remains classified as “sold” in the train’s online system. In addition, if a ticket is purchased for a passenger but they do not board, the person whose ID was used to buy the ticket retains the right to decide how the seat is used.

On Aug. 21, the Chengdu Bureau of China’s National Railway responded to the controversy, seemingly contradicting 12306: “If a passenger fails to board after purchasing a ticket due to personal reasons, the passenger is considered to have forfeited their right to use the seat … according to the rules, the seat cannot be occupied by a third party.” The bureau noted that such instances should be reported to the train staff.

But a day later, the case shifted from a dispute over passengers’ rights and entitlements to discussions on the lack of support for children traveling alone, as well as the difficulties faced by migrant families. The girls’ mother, speaking to domestic media on Aug. 22, explained that she works in Shanghai and was sending her two daughters back to their hometown. She added that she did not have enough time to escort them and wanted them to “develop their independence.” The extra seat, she said, could also serve as a place to lie down for the two, as she worried about male strangers sleeping beside them in sleeper cars.

She also noted that, under ticketing rules, minors cannot buy tickets themselves and their tickets must instead be purchased alongside an adult ticket.

In a commentary, The Paper wrote that “behind the purchase of the three tickets lies a harsh reality faced by millions of working families, leaving migrant families with no alternative.” It recommended that the railway system follow airlines — which allow parents to apply for service for unaccompanied minors in advance — as an example.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A video screenshot shows the empty seat that gave rise to a national debate. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018902/China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018902/China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.content:
Editor’s note: This is the first of a two-part series on how AI is reshaping China’s ultrashort-drama industry.

HENAN, Central China — When a tow truck stopped beside three luxury cars at Zhoutu Culture’s compound in the central Chinese city of Zhengzhou in July, crew members assumed they were headed to another shoot.

Zhoutu was shooting so many ultrashort dramas that the company calculated owning the cars would eventually cost less than renting them as props, and bring some tax savings. Founder Wang Huan and his business partners had each chosen a model they had long wanted.

But the Mercedes-Benz G63, Aston Martin DB11, and Bentley Continental GT were leaving for good. Zhoutu sold all three for a combined 4.5 million yuan ($650,000).

Wang photographed the three cars before they left and posted the images on social media with the caption: “Selling cars and all in short dramas.”

“Of course it stirred up some emotions,” he later told Sixth Tone. “But it wasn’t anything like what people might imagine — like feeling we’d gone bankrupt or something.”

Within months of adding the cars to its fleet, Zhoutu’s output had plunged from as many as 200 ultrashort dramas a month to around 30. Its full-time workforce had fallen from more than 500 employees at its 2025 peak to around 200. More than 20,000 costumes had been moved to a nearby building as an AI studio took over their former space. Even the canteen was closed.

Beyond Zhoutu’s gates, shoots were disappearing across Zhengzhou, one of China’s largest ultrashort-drama production hubs, often dubbed the country’s “Vertical Hollywood.”

The smartphone-first dramas, typically told in episodes lasting only a minute or two, reached 851 million users across China by May, in an industry now worth more than 100 billion yuan. Major platforms fueled the boom with scripts, guaranteed funding, and incentives for producers that could deliver at scale.

But the production model underpinning the industry’s rise began to unravel in February. AI was rapidly reducing the cost of work that had previously required live-action crews, while major platforms began cutting the guaranteed funding that had helped sustain breakneck expansion.

Across the live-action industry, people began calling it a “winter.”

Shot clock

“Master Comes Down the Mountain, Tasks Me With Wooing His Daughter” is one of the few Zhoutu productions still shooting in July.

In one scene, four armed guards sent by two sisters from a powerful family rush the protagonist, played by Cai Zhongyuan. He waves one hand and sends them sprawling. One draws a gun and fires; Cai catches the bullet between two fingers.

Director Li Jun adds both flourishes on set, giving the hero two more moments of triumph typical of male-oriented ultrashort dramas.

Cai then turns his attention back to the sisters, whom he had earlier encountered while they were bathing, and continues flirting with them. When the elder sister finally loses her temper and slaps him, the two collide — and kiss.

Li steps away from the monitor before the kiss. “Don’t pull away too quickly. Three seconds. Separate only after I say so,” she tells the leads. She adjusts a side light, tells the camera operator to shoot in slow motion, then calls action.

“Perfect.” In just three takes, the drama’s most important romantic scene is finished.

“Master Comes Down the Mountain” will eventually run for around 100 minutes. Li has three days to shoot it, on a budget of roughly 200,000 yuan.

Barely 160 centimeters tall, with cropped hair and a voice that carries across the set, she keeps the production moving almost without pause.

When crew chatter continues as the cameras are about to roll, Li cuts across it: “Why don’t you chat in front of the camera instead?” A stalled fog machine, missing prop, or crew member drifting into frame brings another rebuke.

“For simple shots like this, don’t come back to me asking what to do,” she tells the assistant director, pushing the crew to keep routine shots moving without waiting for her.

A comparable production last year would have cost around 300,000 yuan and taken seven or eight days, Li says. The roughly 30-person core filming crew has remained largely intact, but around 10 jobs tied to stunt work and special effects have been cut after related scenes were removed or shifted to AI.

At her busiest, Li directed roughly four dramas a month. From preparation to release, she says, an ultrashort production could take less than a month, with crews routinely working 14 to 16 hours a day.

Wang Ruoyan, 24, who plays the elder sister in “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” remembers getting only around 10 hours of sleep during one five-day shoot as lunch breaks disappeared into costume and makeup changes.

“I even fell asleep in the shower once,” she says. “When I woke up, 30 minutes had passed.”

Wang also saw actors carrying quick-acting heart medication on set. Li says she did the same during especially intense periods, urging actors on her crews to keep some with them to “save their lives.”

Last summer, Li recalled ambulances arriving three times in a single afternoon.

“Some people had acute myocarditis, some suffered heatstroke, and some were simply exhausted from working too hard and staying up too late,” she says. “People would become mentally disoriented, and if they weren’t careful, they could easily fall and get injured.”

On more demanding productions, Li says, actors might finish at 3 or 4 a.m. and be back on set four hours later.

“No one has the energy or passion to create,” Li says. “They’re just thinking about finishing, getting off work, and going to sleep.”

Luo Haoyu, an actor who frequently worked with Li, was on set as many as 28 days a month at the height of the boom. Some nights, he filmed until 5 a.m., then rushed straight to another shoot without even removing his makeup.

“Deep down, everyone knew those crazy days wouldn’t last forever,” Luo says. “We were burning ourselves out because everyone understood that last year was an exceptional period for short dramas.”

Hard landing

Those “crazy days” lasted until February.

That month, TikTok owner ByteDance released Seedance 2.0, an AI video model capable of generating increasingly polished footage for around 1 yuan per second.

Soon after, Hongguo — ByteDance’s ultrashort-drama platform and a major source of scripts and financing — began withdrawing guaranteed funding from many small and midsize live-action projects.

The shift hit companies like Zhoutu particularly hard: three years earlier, a Hongguo-backed rebirth melodrama, “My Daughter Pulled the Plug on My Oxygen Tank,” had given the company its breakout hit, generating more than 10 million yuan in user spending on its first day.

“The landing was extremely hard,” says Zhoutu founder Wang Huan.

Zhoutu has since opened a 50-person AI studio, while about 20 live-action directors also work on AI productions. It makes six to eight AI dramas a month, largely, Wang says, to “maintain a presence” in the market.

At the same time, the company is using cheaper live-action projects to keep its remaining workforce employed. “With so much investment and so many employees, our strategy is still to operate on a model that keeps more people working,” Wang says. If that fails, he says, Zhoutu may shrink further.

The company had already spent nearly two months after the Spring Festival, in mid-February, with little work coming in. “When you don’t know what to do, the safest option is to stop,” Wang says. “At least you won’t lose more money.”

Productions booked before the downturn kept Li on set for a few weeks. Then new scripts dwindled to roughly one a month, and by April her team had nothing to shoot. Directors around her began moving into AI production, while actors suddenly found themselves waiting for work.

Luo says his monthly income fell from around 20,000 yuan during the boom to roughly 5,000 yuan. In the first three months after the Spring Festival, he worked just 20 days in total.

“I felt confused and lost,” he recalls. “What am I supposed to do in the future?”

He began binge eating, sometimes until he felt he might vomit. For an actor normally careful about his weight, the behavior unsettled him.

“At the time, I thought, things were already this bad. Eating at least made me feel a little better,” he says.

He considered leaving the industry altogether, but could not bring himself to do it. “I still want to see whether audiences can once again have higher expectations for live-action productions,” he says.

Yet producers kept pouring into AI. More than 95% of the 128,000 ultrashort dramas released in the first quarter of 2026 were AI-generated, according to the China Netcasting Services Association (CNSA).

By May, Bytedance pledged 1.5 billion yuan to support live-action short dramas, while six major platforms announced at least 6 billion yuan in planned investment. Regulators also allocated funding for higher-quality productions across 11 provinces.

Live-action output rebounded in the second quarter, partly due to shelved projects returning, though CNSA data shows AI still accounted for 64% of releases.

But Wang is reluctant to bet Zhoutu’s future on another round of platform money. “If Hongguo stopped giving you money tomorrow, what would you do?” he says.

For Shi, a 22-year-old background actor, the slowdown meant days spent waiting for work. During the boom, small speaking roles and regular extra work could bring him close to 10,000 yuan a month. By the time Sixth Tone met him, he had landed just one job in 10 days.

For 110 yuan, Shi spent the morning waiting to appear for a few seconds as a guard: charge at the hero, pretend to be hit, fall to the ground.

He was also still owed 800 yuan from a production the previous December. The company had disappeared, as had the person who recruited him. All Shi had left was their nickname on messaging app WeChat.

“We don’t even know who to ask for our money,” says Shi, who asked to be identified only by his surname. “Construction workers can at least find someone to demand their wages from. With film crews, they’re long gone.”

Shi barely watches live-action ultrashort dramas anymore. He prefers AI-generated comic dramas.

“AI is especially good at stories that rely heavily on visual effects,” he says. “It does those really well.”

Still rolling

For the opening scene of “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” the male lead falls from the sky. Last year, Li says, the crew would have used wire work and spent at least half a day filming it. This time, the actor simply lay face down on a round stone table in front of a small green screen.

“AI can generate all the surrounding scenery,” Li says. “It can make the male lead descend through the clouds, and even create a sweeping aerial shot following him all the way to the ground.”

The whole shot took less than 30 minutes, and Li estimates it saves around 10,000 yuan.

Months earlier, Zhoutu had offered many of its directors the option of switching to AI production. For Li, that meant planning shots and guiding a team through the video-generation process.

After a day or two learning the job, Li says she could already do the work. The pay was about 30% lower. Of roughly 10 directors around her who faced the same choice, eight switched to AI. Li refused.

“Live-action short dramas need a director more,” Li says. “With the right prompt, anyone can make AI videos. But with real filming, you have to work with the actors, camera, and lighting. The sense of achievement is different.”

Zhoutu now rarely makes premium live-action dramas with big budgets. Instead, it focuses on cheaper remakes of proven hits, particularly modern-day rural stories that can be filmed quickly.

“AI’s advantage is making two immortals arguing in the sky, not people arguing outside a village house,” Wang says. A family-conflict drama can cost less than 50,000 yuan to shoot with real actors. Internally, Zhoutu calls these “emotion-driven dramas for lower-tier markets.”

Many of Zhoutu’s remaining live-action productions are male-oriented stories and remakes of plots that have already yielded success. Wang says they can be shot faster than female-oriented dramas, which typically require more time for atmosphere and emotional development.

In one scene from “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” Wang Ruoyan and the second female lead enter the hero’s bedroom in lace and bunny-style nightdresses. Before filming, Li adjusts two strings of hanging round plastic discs. Placed close to the lens, the pieces blur into soft circles of light; she moves them farther apart until the effect sits where she wants it in the frame.

“This is the craftsmanship I only use in female-oriented dramas,” she jokes.

The extra effort does not always pay off. Some of her carefully polished dramas have performed poorly; others that she rushed through became hits.

“Those times make me wonder whether I really understand the market,” she says. “I started doubting myself.”

The final scene of “Master Comes Down the Mountain” has Cai seated at a dinner table as three women, including the two sisters, confess their love. The elder sister tells him to choose one.

“Can’t I have all three?” he replies.

The women rush him, pulling his ears and grabbing his arms as the camera pushes in. Freeze frame.

Although it’s the ending of the drama, it’s filmed on the first day of the three-day shoot. Li still has two days of scenes to get through.

At lunch, she makes the cast a promise: “I’ll do my best to get you back to the hotel by 7 p.m., so you can order takeout from bed.”

“That would be heaven,” Wang Ruoyan says.

Additional reporting: Lü Xiao; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Monitors show a scene being filmed by director Li Jun in Zhengzhou, Henan province, June 2026. Reedited by Ding Yining; photo by Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.title: China Before the Infinite Camera Roll
World.content:
Of the many consumer goods that entered China in the 1980s, one small item transformed how millions of families recorded their lives: 35mm color negative film.

In 1984, Fujifilm established its Beijing office, as Chinese photographers were beginning to embrace the company’s color film, known for its green packaging and the distinctive greenish cast of its prints. Kodak, Fujifilm’s main rival at the time, soon followed, expanding its presence and introducing a network of express color photo stores across China in the 1990s.

These developments, together with the arrival of point-and-shoot cameras that required little skill to achieve proper exposure and sharp focus, enabled ordinary Chinese people to record their lives in color. The film was developed to produce negatives, which were then printed as photographs for family albums.

Not everyone kept the negatives. Many ended up at recycling plants, which is where French artist Thomas Sauvin’s work began. In 2009, Sauvin met Xiaoma, a Beijinger who recovered silver nitrate from X-rays, CDs, and negatives. The two struck a deal, and Sauvin received his first batch of negatives to digitize. Their partnership would eventually help create one of China’s largest private archives of photographic negatives: the Beijing Silvermine.

The project gives broader significance in banal, amateur images. As patterns emerge across dozens, sometimes hundreds, of photographs, personal moments become part of a collective record. One example is a series of portraits taken beside refrigerators, an appliance many Chinese households were acquiring for the first time in the 1990s. Together, such images document the transformation of everyday life as a rapidly changing China became wealthier and more urban.

Much has changed since then. Film gave way to digital cameras, and then to smartphones. People can now easily take thousands of photos a year, a number unthinkable to most families in the 1990s, when a roll of film contained just 36 exposures.

More recently, however, analog photography has enjoyed a revival on social media, where users are drawn to its vintage tones and textures. In 2025, Lucky Film, a Chinese manufacturer that once competed with Kodak and Fujifilm, announced the return of its color negative film amid growing demand from nostalgic millennials and curious Gen Z consumers. Yet a roll of film and lab processing now cost more than 100 yuan (US$14.80) for just 36 photos, leaving analog photography a niche hobby.

The intention behind analog photography has also changed, according to Sauvin. “Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative, and they will post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram,” said Sauvin, who does not shoot film himself.

What has been lost? Humor, perhaps. Looking through the Beijing Silvermine images, it is hard not to be struck by the ease with which people posed and smiled, gazing into the camera with little of the self-consciousness or affectation common in photography today. Before social media, people seemed simply to be enjoying the moments they were living.

In June, Sixth Tone sat down with Sauvin to discuss what analog photography reveals about the lives of ordinary Chinese people in the 1990s and today, his own relationship with the archive, and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence. The interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Sixth Tone: What was your first impression of the earliest batches of recycled negatives, and how did you begin to interpret their meaning?

Sauvin: They were very banal. Quite boring, sometimes very repetitive. It took maybe two or three years before I started to understand what I could do with them. At some point, because of the quantity, you leave the universe of personal stories and enter the universe of collective memory.

A simple example is that, at the beginning of the project, I came across a photo of a woman posing next to a fridge. And I thought, “Oh, having your portrait taken with a fridge is an unusual thing to do.” Then I saw another one, then another one, and now I probably have a series of 25 pictures like this. In the early 1990s, households in Beijing began acquiring refrigerators. They would decorate them and take photos with them. And that’s something no one else would really record. A photojournalist would never make a series about this, nor would a historian or an artist. It’s too close to daily life. It’s too simple. Yet ordinary people, accidentally and unconsciously, capture the bigger picture in these negatives.

Sixth Tone: Is there a single frame or series that interests you most?

Sauvin: So many. I like the photos taken at Beijing World Park. It opened in 1993, and people went there to get a sense of travel, to experience the outside world and its monuments. In the archive, I have thousands of photos taken there in 1993, 1994, and 1995. It was the perfect playground for taking photos. You could have your picture taken with the Twin Towers, the Statue of Liberty, the Eiffel Tower, and so on.

Then, when I went through photos taken in the early 2000s, these Chinese tourists weren’t at the World Park anymore. They were in the actual countries. And when I look at these negatives, as a French person, I always wonder: Is it the real one or the World Park one?

Sixth Tone: Besides the Eiffel Tower series, were there any photos that connected the collection to your own life?

Sauvin: A lot. I was born and raised in Paris, so I’m attentive to photos taken there. I found photos taken on Rue Fabert in the 7th arrondissement, where I learned to walk when I was 1 year old. It’s my home. Seeing someone posing right where I learned to walk was a strange feeling.

I also remember going to the Louvre Museum as a kid and seeing tourists taking photos: flash, flash, flash! Two or three decades later, I started the Silvermine project and found those kinds of photos. Because they were photographing oil paintings with a flash, you always get this big white dot in the image. I made a series about them called “Dazzling Old Masters.”

But the entire archive also has a very strong connection with me. The first time I went to Beijing was in 1999, on a family exchange. In 2009, exactly 10 years later, I started this project, which allowed me to discover the Beijing that existed before I arrived. I wouldn’t have done that with any other city in the world.

Sixth Tone: Have you been able to contact the people in these images?

Sauvin: There’s a photo I found in 2010 that I absolutely love: a young girl posing on a red motorcycle on a street in Dashilar, Beijing. One day, she got in touch with me on Weibo and said, “That girl on the bike, it’s me.” She sent me the printed photo from her family album.

I immediately sent her the other 35 photos from the same roll, and she discovered many that she’d probably never seen because people didn’t always print every photo. Looking through them, she realized that the roll contained four consecutive birthdays, meaning the film had been in the family camera for more than four years. They had to wait that long to finish the roll, have it developed, and finally see the images.

That says a lot about how our relationship with photography has changed and how analog photography captures who we are as human beings in a very pure way. Because it costs money and takes time, you make sure to record the moments that matter. I really like the idea of these latent images sitting in a film canister for four years, then one day being put into chemicals and revealing all these moments. And I find it crazy that, after waiting four years, the negatives could be thrown away the very next day.

Sixth Tone: There is a fine line between the privacy of these images and the public nature of your collection and exhibitions. How do you navigate that tension?

Sauvin: Of course, I’m dealing with very private, intimate photos that were never meant to be used in a book or shown in an exhibition. People are vulnerable because they are themselves. That’s something I always try to keep in mind.

I always make sure not to make fun of people. That’s not easy, because a very important part of the Beijing Silvermine’s visual universe is its sense of humor. There’s something very light, funny, and fresh about it. So you need to preserve that sense of humor because it’s the soul of the project, while never crossing the line into making fun of people.

Another rule I’ve given myself almost since the beginning is that I generally avoid using two images of the same person. That way, I make sure never to delve too deeply into one person’s life. What brings the photos together are more anthropological themes. The photos come together and contribute to a theme. But I would not be comfortable showing many photos taken by the same person.

In 2015, a very good friend of mine in Beijing came to me with a big cardboard box containing all the negatives and photos of her late father. He took a lot of photos and organized everything very neatly, with handwritten information everywhere: Here are the 120 films; there are the 35mm films. It was absolutely beautiful.

She gave it to me and said, “I think you’re doing great things with negatives, so this is yours, and just do what you want with it.” I was never able to open the box a second time because it was not my place to deal with this material. It all comes from one person. I know who this person is, so I can do absolutely nothing with it.

Sixth Tone: How do your curatorial decisions reflect the way you view analog photographs within their historical context?

Sauvin: In this exhibition, curated by Holly Russell at Fotografiska Shanghai, we present one room with 1,300 prints. That’s the selection I’ve been working on for 16 years. The selection was organized around themes, topics, and angles that emerged organically from the archive.

But when we brought the archive to Shanghai, we decided not to present each series together. Everything is mixed, so it’s up to the viewer to look at the photos and, just like I did, start seeing connections between them. I also didn’t decide which photo would go where. They were hung quite randomly by the workers who installed the show, and some amazing connections happened simply because of that.

We also decided to present everything as 10-by-15-centimeter prints, which is probably the size of the prints that would have been made from these negatives for family albums. No photo is bigger than another, so we’re not claiming that one is more important. What makes them powerful is their coming together.

There’s something about found photography, about vernacular photography, that is completely crazy: Quantity is more important than quality. You need quantity to make the switch from personal memory to collective memory. That’s how you end up with a gigantic photo album. It’s not the album of a family. It’s the album of a city, a generation, a place, and a time.

Sixth Tone: We have seen a resurgence of analog photography recently, globally but especially in China. Lucky Film is producing color negative film again. What do you make of this renewed interest? Why do you think it appeals to young Chinese people?

Sauvin: I suppose it’s about our relationship with the medium. We’re always drawn to technologies from the past. We’ve seen this with music. We had vinyl records, then CDs, MiniDiscs, and MP3s, and now we are going back to vinyl. There is a worldwide trend of people going back to analog photography. I’m not sure I’m very interested in that. Now we’re at a stage where we’re mass-producing images, and I’d rather live in my time and do that than go back to an earlier, previous tool.

And there’s something very different. People 30 years ago were shooting analog, but there was no artistic intention or intention to share these photos online. There wasn’t this element of staging or representation.

Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative and post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram. So the intention is not pure. In the end, what does it mean? It means it’s a filter, like a vintage filter of some kind. That’s why I’m not very interested in the trend. I love analog photography, but it died about 20 years ago.

Sixth Tone: Artificial intelligence is being used to restore and recreate faded or damaged negatives. Do you see it primarily as a boon or a bane?

Sauvin: I find it completely fascinating, and I’m sure that, combined with the right idea, it could be an amazing tool. I’m really open to it.

That being said, I need to be very careful because I have this Silvermine archive of 1 million photos, all made of flesh and blood, that come from ordinary people. They are physical objects, and for so many years, when I scanned a photo and shared it, people trusted that the photo existed. There was no question about that.

Then suddenly, about a year ago, we had this explosion of AI-generated images, and it changed people’s minds, mine as well. Now when you see a photo, the first question you ask yourself is: Is it real, or is it AI?

I really don’t want that confusion to happen with the Silvermine. I want to make it very clear: I deal only with analog photography, and I do not modify the photos in any way.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018923/China’s First Booster Landing Marks Leap Toward Reusable Rockets
World.title: China’s First Booster Landing Marks Leap Toward Reusable Rockets
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018923/China’s First Booster Landing Marks Leap Toward Reusable Rockets
World.content:
China has landed an orbital rocket’s booster, rather than discarding it, for the first time, paving the way for sustainable rocket launches and potentially cutting future launches’ costs by tens of millions of yuan.

The Aug. 19 milestone by Chinese aerospace startup LandSpace also makes China the second country after the U.S. to successfully recover rocket boosters on both solid ground and at sea — the latter feat accomplished last month.

U.S.-based aerospace companies SpaceX and Blue Origin were previously the only enterprises to have successfully landed rocket boosters on solid ground. SpaceX has also recovered boosters at sea — by landing them vertically on drone ships — compared with China’s net-capture method.

On Wednesday at 7:35 am, the 66.1-meter-tall Zhuque-3 lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Pilot Zone in the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, and delivered an internet satellite into its designated orbit.

The rocket’s stainless-steel booster, carrying nine liquid oxygen-methane engines, later landed 390 kilometers away in neighboring Gansu province.

A similar attempt by the same company on Dec. 3 last year failed following combustion. On the latest model, the team improved the landing propulsion system and added protective structures, domestic media reported.

China’s push to build extensive low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks — “megaconstellations” of coordinated satellites operating 2,000 kilometers or less above Earth — is driving growing demand for cheaper, more frequent rocket launches.

Such networks aim to provide services such as high-speed internet access in remote areas. The country currently has a few hundred satellites in orbit, and tens of thousands are ultimately planned.

A rocket’s booster, located at the bottom of the ship and used in the initial stage of launch, is commonly the most expensive component, accounting for 70% or more of a rocket’s hardware costs, LandSpace told domestic media. Traditionally, however, they are discarded after launch, leaving the upper part of the rocket to continue toward orbit.

Reuse of a common nine-engine booster could save at least 20 million to 50 million yuan ($2.9 million to $7.4 million), Zhang Liang, technical lead of a reusable rocket research team at Sun Yat-sen University’s School of Aeronautics and Astronautics, told domestic media.

However, Zhang added that China still faces a shortage of launch facilities. The cost advantage of reusable rockets will only become significant if there are enough launches for rockets to be reused multiple times a year.

According to LandSpace, the cost per launch could fall by about 45% after five uses. The Zhuque-3’s first stage is designed to be reused at least 20 times, with the company ultimately aiming to bring launch costs below 20,000 yuan per kilogram of payload.

LandSpace told domestic media that it plans to relaunch the recovered booster as soon as possible.

Over the past decade, supportive policies from the central government have led more private companies to enter China’s space sector, which state-owned enterprises previously dominated.

Last November, the China National Space Administration released a two-year action plan pledging to expand access to rocket testing facilities and strengthen international cooperation. The space sector is also listed as a strategic priority in China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, which began this year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 rocket booster lands in Minqin, Gansu province, Aug. 19, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018922/Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.title: Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018922/Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.content:
Chinese supermarket chain Pangdonglai has announced the recruitment of former convicts for the second year in a row, expanding its hiring scope to employees who have spent at least five years in prison. The move has sparked renewed debate over the line between reducing employment discrimination against former inmates and upholding public safety.

The plan, announced Aug. 14 by the company’s branch in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, involves recruiting 20 people who have served sentences of at least five years. The store is set to open in October.

Pangdonglai was founded by Yu Donglai in 1995. Based in Henan’s Xuchang City, it has gained a reputation for offering relatively high pay, shorter working hours, and generous time off — emphasizing employee well-being over profit.

Employees work no more than 36 hours per week — in China, the legal limit is 40 hours — and receive 40 days of paid leave annually, including 10 “mental health” days. In the first quarter of 2026, employees’ average monthly salary was 9,600 yuan ($1,400), compared with roughly 5,800 yuan at China’s private wholesale and retail businesses.

Last year, the company recruited former convicts for the first time. Applicants were required to have served no more than 10 years in prison, be under the age of 35, and have a middle school education or higher.

Yu said in a Saturday post on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, that all 30 former convicts hired last year remain employed by the company.

This year, the company looks to recruit former inmates who have served sentences of at least five years.

The move quickly divided opinion online. Supporters praised the company for giving convicts a second chance. Lin Minming, founder of Red Apple Public Welfare, an organization that supports the children of prisoners, told domestic media that the company’s decision to continue hiring ex-convicts, particularly those who “may be facing even more difficult employment challenges,” is “worth paying attention to.”

“In the past, people would make baseless assumptions when talking about this issue — worrying that former inmates would be difficult to manage, unstable, or likely to cause problems,” Lin said. “Now that there’s at least a group of real (ex-convicts) working in a real company, we can see what happens.”

Former inmates in China face significant barriers to finding jobs. Fewer than 40% secure employment because of their criminal records, according to local media.

But others raised concerns. “Many people serving more than five years (in prison) were convicted of serious crimes,” one user wrote online. “Supermarkets are crowded places frequented by ordinary people, including children and the elderly. People who have turned their lives around deserve a second chance, but customer safety should not be overlooked.”

Others argued that giving special opportunities to former inmates is unfair to those who have always obeyed the law.

Responding to the concerns, the company told domestic media that people convicted of sexual or violent offenses are ineligible, and that applicants with nonviolent offenses will be prioritized. It added that those hired will initially be assigned to back-office positions such as warehousing and logistics, rather than customer-facing jobs, and undergo a six-month trial period.

China has been strengthening support for former inmates returning to society. A revised Prison Law, passed in April and set to take effect this November, states that discriminating against former convicts in employment, education, or social security matters is illegal.

Former inmates will also be required to undergo “pre-release education” — including legal and psychological counseling, vocational training, and daily-life skills — encouraging them to pursue employment and entrepreneurship.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Customers crowd a Pangdonglai supermarket in Xuchang, Henan province, May 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018916/Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.title: Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018916/Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.content:
Two gray-green production lines glow beneath harsh white lights, their conveyor belts moving ceaselessly like mechanical rivers. Clanging metal, the rip of packing tape, and the dull thud of cardboard boxes mingle with the hurried footsteps of workers shuttling goods back and forth.



It’s July 10, and the Pinotec electric fan factory in Suzhou, in the eastern Jiangsu province, is running at full capacity to meet several rush orders that have come from Europe in the wake of a record-breaking heat wave.

As temperatures soared in June, exports of Chinese air conditioners to the European Union jumped nearly 73% year on year, according to China’s General Administration of Customs. Sales of fans and evaporative air coolers also surged on global e-commerce platforms.

For the managers and employees at Pinotec, which manufactures fans under the Booster brand, the extreme weather represented a lifeline. After taking a major hit from the China-U.S. trade war and the ongoing Middle East conflict, the sudden spike in orders gave the company an opportunity to expand into European markets and turn its finances around.

But as demand has risen, so have the costs of metals and electrical components, while the market competition has rapidly intensified. Add a weakening euro against the yuan — which erodes the value of European revenue when converted back home — and the factory’s profits remain razor-thin.

Despite the hot market, Pinotec and other small- and medium-sized businesses in China are facing the cold, hard reality that this summer boom could leave them weaker, not stronger.

Final countdown

Every hour, factory manager Zhu Guangshuai anxiously paces through the workshop to gauge his workers’ progress. For the past two weeks, Pinotec has been rushing to complete an order for 500 large fans from a customer in Germany — and shipment is scheduled for 8 p.m. tonight.

Zhu had been confident that just two hours would be enough time for final assembly, but the first hour is already gone and only 223 units are finished. To speed things up, he opens a second, smaller production line, initially assigning two additional workers to help with wiring and soldering, before eventually asking the floor supervisor and materials handler to also step in.

In the end, 15 workers drop what they are doing to help their colleagues reach the finish line — attaching screens, installing handle grips, snapping on base plates, tightening screws. Then, they all proceed to packaging.

Multi-skilled workers who can easily switch between roles have become essential for the factory’s survival in recent times. When the Chinese fan market contracted last year, the company merged two assembly lines and laid off any inexperienced or temporary workers, halving its workforce to just 60.

Away from the factory floor, Pinotec also shut down its 40-person domestic e-commerce operation, dispensed with its content creation team for Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, and dismantled its livestreaming studio.

The company initially made massage guns but switched to manufacturing electric fans in late 2023, focusing on high-powered turbo blowers before introducing a range that includes a palm-sized, handheld model. Profits rose early on, but sales dropped sharply once domestic competitors started to flood the market with cheaper alternatives.

Pinotec’s main markets are North America and Europe, where many people commonly use turbo blowers to clean debris from their cars or backyards. Domestic demand is extremely limited. When trade tensions between China and the United States escalated last year, disrupting global markets, 90% of the factory’s orders came from overseas.

Shortly after the U.S. introduced increased tariffs on Chinese exports in February 2025, an American supermarket chain canceled an order for tens of thousands of units. Then, European customers began asking to delay shipments until the economic outlook became clearer.

The company began losing more than 100,000 yuan ($14,835) a month — and that’s before the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East in February this year. Pinotec lost contact with its customers in Iran for almost six months; finished goods piled up in its warehouse, unable to be shipped or paid for.

Things only began to pick up in late May when Europe was hit by an extreme heat wave, with temperatures soaring as high as 45 degrees Celsius in some parts of Spain.

Inquiries flooded in through Pinotec’s international e-commerce platform: A customer in the United Kingdom ordered 2,500 turbo blowers, along with several handheld models; a Belgian distributor placed five orders over two months, totaling more than 2,000 fans, most bound for France; and other units were also shipped to Switzerland and the Netherlands.

To handle the additional workload, the factory reconfigured its production line. Normally, the assembled fans would undergo two days of charge-and-discharge testing, yet Zhu arranged for assembly and testing to be carried out simultaneously, allowing packaging to begin much earlier.

At 8 p.m. on July 10, the fans bound for Germany are shipped on time.

But Zhu barely has time to catch his breath before a new crisis arises. The electric control boards needed for tomorrow’s production order still haven’t arrived after three weeks of waiting. Pinotec has no option but to absorb the pressure. “We’re already right up against the delivery deadline,” Zhu says. “There’s no room to push it back.”

He decides to adjust the production schedule and bring forward another order. The company can’t afford to leave the assembly line idle for even a day.

And the problems keep coming. Whether it’s the time crunch or reduced staffing, defective products keep appearing on the line and need replacing, while a consignment of plastic casings from an upstream supplier is discovered to have color discrepancies between the upper and lower halves.

All Zhu can do is think on his feet to find solutions.

Changing market

According to Pinotec’s founder, Shen Guangping, the combined effects of rising material costs — prices for copper, iron, zinc, tin, lithium batteries, chips, resistors, and capacitors have all increased in 2026 — and fluctuations in the euro-yuan exchange rate have slashed profits by up to 20%.

Deliveries from component suppliers have also become unpredictable. Suppliers used to stockpile some materials, he says, but now no one is willing to hold inventory; materials are procured only after a customer places an order, affecting lead time.

Sometimes, electronic components suddenly increase in price on the same day an order is placed — but once a quote has been given, the factory often has no choice but to absorb the difference.

Pinotec has taken on nearly 200,000 yuan worth of business without passing on the additional material costs, Shen says. “Our sales volume has grown by more than 50% compared with last year, but there’s almost no profit. We’re mainly producing these orders to win new customers and maintain production volume.”

To drum up new business, Shen has been attending as many overseas trade shows as possible. Last year, he attended nearly 20 across the U.S., Germany, Brazil, and Japan. This year his target is 26, at least two a month.

At recent events, he noticed more customers asking about handheld fans. Sensing an opportunity, he began taking small Booster fans to trade shows and had his technical team develop a mini fan and other new products.

However, the market competition is now fierce. Fan manufacturers in Foshan and Zhongshan, two major manufacturing bases in the southern Guangdong province, have orders through September. Domestic factories are also adapting to international requirements, releasing new product colors and developing low-power, variable-frequency models tailored to European voltage standards and electricity costs.

The EU has imposed strict compliance controls on imported cooling products, and incomplete product certification can expose companies to multiple penalties.

Production cycle

It’s been exactly a week since the Pinotec workers rushed to complete the German order, and now they are halfway through assembling a batch of small handheld fans bound for Japan, which has also experienced extreme heat this year.

Suddenly, the production line is halted. An ultrasonic welding mold that fuses the plastic casing is malfunctioning, leaving scorch marks and gaps in the seams.

Zhu assigns a worker to adjust the mold while coordinating others to assemble the remaining components. Fortunately, the problem has come toward the end of the process — any earlier and the day’s production plan would need to be canceled. Just 24 hours earlier, the factory manager was forced to send workers home early due to a battery shortage.

However, when two representatives from the Japanese client later arrive to inspect the goods, they find the mold still hasn’t been repaired, and delivery is postponed.

As an on-site inspector, Du Kai’s task is to report and handle challenges like these. Before joining Pinotec in early 2024, the 28-year-old worked in sales in Beijing and the neighboring city of Tianjin, and as a property agent in the central Henan province. Rather than relying on commission, he had hoped factory work would provide him and his wife more stability.

After proving his versatility, Du was among those who kept his job when the company swung the axe in 2025. Another group that the company was reluctant to let go was its three qualified solderers, as the role requires delicate skill.

Feng Juan is the factory’s most recent hire. Once a temporary worker employed to apply glue, she was recruited as a solderer after someone else quit. In addition to the salary, the job comes with a 1,000 yuan monthly supplement, yet Feng was hesitant at first — she’d heard that the fumes from soldering were toxic and could affect fertility.

She thought it over, and as she already had two sons and wasn’t planning on having more children, she accepted. Her husband runs a lifting equipment installation business, earning 30,000 yuan a month, but Feng says the family still feels financial pressure. In the past year, the couple has renovated a condominium in their native Henan for their eldest son, and is now planning to buy one for their youngest.

Feng’s eldest son, in his late teens, also works at a factory in Suzhou — a temporary arrangement after he began acting out in school — yet she hopes he won’t end up toiling in a high-stress manual job like her.

Packaging line supervisor Wang Chao is also working to save money for his child. A 38-year-old single father, his parents care for his son back in Henan. He no longer has lofty career aspirations, nor is he interested in job-hopping in search of a better position. His only wish is to put away 5,000 yuan a month and have social insurance coverage.

Even as orders have surged, Wang’s packaging team has dwindled to only 12 workers. He hopes to hire five more, but finding them is proving hard. His two recent hires lasted just six days before quitting because the job was “too tiring.”

Zhu and the factory workers are trying to make the most of this summer boom and, in turn, bring more stability to their lives. They hope that, by evening, their finished fans are loaded onto the trucks and shipped overseas on time. Then, the next day, they can do it all again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Du Kai is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Wei Ronghuan.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Workers pack items at the factory in Suzhou, Jiangsu province, July 2026. Lü Meng/White Night Workshop )

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.title: What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.content:
What if the zombie apocalypse was already here?

In the late 2010s, Chinese indie band Hardcore Raver in Tears imagined just such a world in “Take Her to Wanda Plaza,” a jagged, synth-heavy sendup of the country’s mindless consumer culture. Over pounding beats, singer Lu Yan sang of zombified shoppers and took aim at Wang Sicong, the scion of the Wanda real estate empire and one of the most infamous of China’s “second-generation rich.”

The joke landed because Wanda Plaza is more than a shopping mall; by the 2010s, it had become shorthand for a particular vision of urban life. In the 2000s, local governments across the country saw real estate and urbanization as key engines of economic growth as well as fiscal revenue. Teaming with developers like Wanda, they built vast new tracts of standardized residential districts across the country. These new neighborhoods needed new stores and restaurants, a niche that Wanda also filled by building over 500 Wanda Plaza malls in more than 200 cities nationwide.

At the time, this was all taken for granted as modernization in action. China was urbanizing at a staggering speed, and clean, convenient, and air-conditioned shopping malls like Wanda Plaza were welcomed by both the country’s rising middle class and brands hungry to tap an emerging market.

But for the generation that came of age during this transformation, the convenience and prosperity of the new urban landscape is increasingly tinged with a sense of sameness. Rapid urban expansion did not just change how Chinese cities looked, they argue; it also displaced what anthropologist Xiang Biao calls the “nearby”: the small-scale places and relationships immediately around us through which everyday life acquires meaning.

That longing has since found an outlet online. From obsessively documenting faded Y2K architecture to creating virtual cities and nostalgic video games, young Chinese are attempting to recreate an idealized virtual version of the turn-of-the-millennium city: chaotic but colorful, and full of corner shops, wet markets, arcades, street stalls, and other places to hang out.

The most obvious example of this trend is Chinese dreamcore, which blends aspects of the global dreamcore subculture with elements drawn from China’s own millennial moment. The walking simulator “There Exists Nobody,” for example, invites players to revisit China’s bustling millennium-era towns, where neighborhoods were filled with unpolished mom-and-pop shops rather than sleek shopping malls.

A more sophisticated case is artist Huang Heshan’s digital metropolis “Too Rich City,” which he dubbed a work of “socialist cyberpunk.” Drawing on Huang’s experiences growing up in the southern province of Guangdong, the virtual city mixes modern LED screens with nostalgic elephant slides and swan-shaped boats — both recurring motifs in Chinese dreamcore.

Similarly, Liu Yujia, a photographer better known by his social media handle, “Tiehe West Street,” has built a large following for his dreamcore-style documentation of China’s long-maligned Y2K architecture.

When asked why his work resonates with so many, Huang commented that China’s millennial buildings — many of which have been allowed to fall into disrepair — nevertheless remain vibrant in ways the newer, more uniform apartment blocks aren’t. They’re “a little chaotic, but also more human,” he explained.

Indeed, a key motive of Chinese dreamcore is a desire for more human-scale spaces. Cookie-cutter blocks of shopping malls, chain stores, and gated residential communities have smoothed the rough edges of many Chinese cities, yet their lack of texture — places with which people can establish organic connections — has also led to widespread disorientation and disillusionment.

It is in this context that the “nearby,” the academic term popularized by Xiang, has entered public discourse in recent years. Rather than accepting the numbing comfort offered by places like Wanda Plaza, China’s younger generation is searching for informal spaces and trying to rebuild tight-knit communities.

Standardized urban planning, alongside an increasingly digital economy, has also reshaped people’s sense of time. In 2000, an ordinary Chinese person might experience time through walking to a grocery store, a school, or a park. Nowadays, such embodied experience has been replaced by the “estimated time of arrival” displayed in food delivery and car-hailing apps. This abstraction has rendered interpersonal relationships likewise abstract and fragile, contributing to the desire to return to a slower, less hectic era.

It’s worth noting that Chinese dreamcore is not the only space where the younger generation is seeking shelter and trying to build a digital “nearby.” The anime and fandom subcultures, for example, offer a similar sense of belonging.

Much of this can be traced back to worldwide trends like the loss of “third places” where young people can hang out away from parents and teachers, forcing them into online spaces increasingly divorced from their physical surroundings and leading to what the scholar Keith Hayward calls a culture of “self-infantilization” — such as the global social media craze for kitsch toys like Labubu.

It’s not hard to see why dreamcore-tinged nostalgia would find such fertile ground in both the West and China, even if one romanticizes malls while the other rejects them. These online trends have limits, however. Loosely organized, they lack the capability to make an impact offline. Meanwhile, some of the very offline spaces dreamcore fans like to criticize have effectively incorporated the subculture, positioning themselves as a new kind of “nearby.” Shopping hubs such as Shanghai’s Bailian mall and Beijing’s Wangfujing street now host regular events for anime fans, while Changsha’s Wenheyou has redecorated its commercial complexes to look like vintage markets and evoke feelings of “old Changsha.”

Ultimately, Y2K nostalgia is not immune to the consumerism it seeks to reject. With mounting financial pressure for commercial real estate developers, the Wanda Plaza model may have passed its heyday. Yet the urban landscape it has imposed upon us seems likely to last. They may complain about monotonous “new districts” and their lack of organic street life, but young Chinese continue to find the convenience that modern cities offer irresistible. Chinese dreamcore provides a temporary relief — sooner or later, though, we’re snapped awake by the buzz of our phones.

(Header image: 500px/VCG)

World.content:
DEMONSTRATION. Students hold a protest at the University of the Philippines Cebu to denounce government corruption and political dynasties on February 19, 2026.

The University of the Philippines System has a proposed allocation of P26.53 billion for next year, which is lower than the funding it received in the 2026 national budget

MANILA, Philippines – The Marcos administration wants to provide P134.56 billion as funding for state universities and colleges (SUCs) in 2027, down from the 2026 budget of P137.9 billion.

Including funding for retirement and life insurance premiums — an automatic appropriation or item already authorized by existing legislation — the figure would go up to P141.09 billion, according to the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

If the proposed allocation for the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) is added, the budget for higher education next year would be at P176.5 billion. (READ: Top 10 agencies with biggest allocations in proposed 2027 budget)

At the granular level, the country’s 113 SUCs would have different fates.

The University of the Philippines (UP) System has P26.53 billion under the 2027 NEP, lower than the P29.47 billion it got in the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA).

The UP System’s budget last year was the largest it has ever received.

The Hospital Services Program, where funding for the UP-Philippine General Hospital is sourced, is seen to have a budget cut next year.

Under the 2027 NEP, the program is allocated P7.29 billion, an P805-million reduction from its P8.1-billion budget under the 2026 GAA.

Funds for the university’s Research Program may also be slashed next year, as it is only allocated P829.61 million under the 2027 NEP, a significant decrease from the P1.76 billion under this year’s national budget.

Here are the proposed allocations for the other programs of the UP System under the 2027 NEP:

Higher Education Program – P11.69 billion

Advanced Education Program – P1.92 billion

Technical Advisory Extension Program – P445 million

In a Palace press briefing on August 13, Presidential Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro said budget adjustments depend on the projects scheduled for a certain year. Castro said this was the explanation she got from the Department of Budget and Management.

Listed below are the proposed 2027 budgets of the 113 SUCs.

Meanwhile, the government is seeking a P61-billion allocation for the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Program, which provides free tuition to qualified students enrolled in SUCs, local universities and colleges, and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority institutions.

For next year, the Marcos administration would like to set aside P1.6 billion for the Bagong Pilipinas Merit Scholarship Program, lodged under CHED, to support 20,000 continuing scholars and 10,000 new beneficiaries.

Budget deliberations are ongoing at the House appropriations committee level. – Rappler.com

World.title: Acosta grilled over scrutiny of OVP confidential funds receipts
World.content:
SCRUTINY. Former special disbursing officer of the Office of the Vice President Gina Acosta testifies as a hostile witness during the impeachment trial of Sara Duterte on August 17, 2026.

Senator-judges grill former Office of the Vice President special disbursing officer Gina Acosta on the level of due diligence she exercised in examining the documentary evidence for confidential funds liquidation

MANILA, Philippines – Gina Acosta, who served as the special disbursing officer (SDO) of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for its P125-million confidential funds in 2022, faced intense scrutiny from senator-judges on Monday, August 24, over how she examined the documentary evidence used to liquidate the controversial funds.

On Day 17 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, senator-judges questioned Acosta on the extent of her due diligence in scrutinizing the acknowledgement receipts that Colonel Raymund Dante Lachica, former security head of the OVP, submitted in liquidating the confidential funds.

Acosta repeatedly told the court that she merely disbursed the funds and that it was Lachica who implemented the programs under the funds. She also admitted relying on the documents and Lachica’s assurances about verifying the use of the confidential funds despite having no personal knowledge of the transactions.

“Kasi siya po ang may alam. Siya po ang nag-implement. Siya po ang nag-implement sa mga projects sa confidential (Because he’s the one who knows about it. He was the one who implemented the projects under the confidential funds),” Acosta told the impeachment court.

During the trial, the House prosecution panel said more unusual names appeared in the acknowledgment receipts, including “Pagong,” “Pusa,” and “Ngitngit.” They also flagged Acosta’s seemingly “templated” answers, as well as her reliance on Lachica in verifying the transactions.

Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo asked Acosta why she did not scrutinize the receipts more closely despite the use of such unusual names.

“Kasi siya po ang nag-implement sa mga confidential activities, Your Honor, on the grounds. Siya po ang inatasan na mag-implement. Siya po ang nag….siya ang implementor po, Your Honor,” she said.

(He implemented the confidential activities, Your Honor, on the ground. He was tasked to implement them. He was the implementor, Your Honor.)

Other senator-judges raised similar questions, including Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III, who, at one point, cut short his interjection and said: “Ayoko na marinig ang template (I don’t want to hear the template anymore).”

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros, for her part, asked Acosta whether she thought it would be fair if she ended up taking the fall for the alleged misuse of the funds in her capacity as an accounting officer.

“Alam ko po, Ma‘am, na alam po ni Ma’am Vice President Sara Duterte ang ginagawa niya (I know that Vice President Sara Duterte knows what she is doing),” Acosta said.

The prosecution presented Acosta as a witness for Article I of the articles of impeachment against Duterte, which accuses the Vice President of misusing P612.5 million in confidential funds of the OVP and the Department of Education (DepEd).

Edward Fajarda’s health

During the trial, the impeachment court confirmed receipt of a letter from the lawyers of former DepEd SDO Edward Fajarda informing the court that he suffered from a brain stroke and cannot testify in the trial.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero instructed the Senate medical bureau to examine Fajarda and validate the medical findings before excusing him from the trial.

“The court notes the medical certificate from counsel and physician of Mr. Fajarda. However, before we excuse him as requested, the court is instructing and directing the head of the Senate’s medical and dental bureau, Dr. Sison, to examine the witness and validate the medical findings with his physicians and submit a report to this court regarding his condition and if he indeed he will be unable to testify this week and when, if at all, he can testify,” Escudero said. – Rappler.com
